0: Not this: Medications belong to the SAMPLE history, gathered after life threats are handled.
Not this: Vital signs come after the primary assessment has found and treated life threats.
Not this: Listening to lung sounds is part of the later, more detailed assessment of breathing.
Correct: With the scene safe, the primary assessment starts with a general impression of age, distress and obvious life threats.
1: Not this: The primary assessment only confirms ventilation is adequate; methodical auscultation of every lung field waits until life threats are handled.
Correct: Systematic bilateral auscultation of the chest is part of the secondary assessment, after immediate life threats have been managed.
Not this: Lung sounds are useful in any patient with a breathing complaint, responsive or not, so responsiveness does not decide this.
Not this: Scene size-up happens before patient contact, so no hands-on exam such as auscultation can take place then.
2: Correct: No response to voice but withdrawal from a painful stimulus places the patient at P on the AVPU scale.
Not this: Unresponsive means no response to any stimulus, and this patient pulled his arm away.
Not this: Alert means awake and aware without any stimulus.
Not this: Verbal means he responds when spoken to, which he did not.
3: Not this: Mental status is checked with AVPU or GCS in the primary assessment and is not a SAMPLE letter.
Not this: Past medical history is the P in SAMPLE (pertinent past history), not the M.
Not this: Mechanism of injury is judged at scene size-up and is not one of the SAMPLE letters.
Correct: M is Medications, which can explain the presentation or interact with treatments you might give.
4: Not this: The ankle itself still needs an exam, including distal pulse, motor function and sensation, before you treat it.
Correct: An alert patient with an isolated injury and no significant mechanism gets an exam focused on the injured area.
Not this: The exam is chosen from how the patient presents now, not held back in case he later loses consciousness.
Not this: A rapid full-body exam is for significant mechanisms, multi-system trauma or altered mental status, none of which apply here.
5: Correct: A SAMPLE history needs patient contact and belongs to history taking, so it is the one item that is not part of size-up.
Not this: BSI and standard precautions are a size-up component, taken before patient contact.
Not this: Determining the mechanism of injury or nature of illness is a core part of size-up.
Not this: Scene safety is a core size-up component and the first thing confirmed.
6: Correct: Knowing the patient count early lets you request more ambulances or declare an MCI before you are committed to one patient.
Not this: Who writes the report has nothing to do with why patients are counted.
Not this: Destination is driven by patient condition and protocol, not mainly by patient count.
Not this: Documentation and billing are distant secondary uses compared with getting resources moving early.
7: Correct: The general impression is formed in seconds from what is visible on approach: age, sex, distress and obvious life threats.
Not this: Laboratory results are hospital data and play no part in the field impression.
Not this: Vital signs are taken after the primary assessment, not before the first impression.
Not this: The SAMPLE history is gathered later, during the secondary assessment.
8: Not this: That describes the EMT's clinical impression, which is the provider's interpretation and is documented separately from the complaint.
Not this: Mechanism of injury describes how a trauma happened, not what the patient says is wrong.
Correct: The chief complaint is the patient's own stated reason for calling, ideally recorded in their words.
Not this: Vital signs are objective measurements, while the chief complaint is the patient's subjective statement.
9: Correct: OPQRST walks through onset, provocation, quality, radiation, severity and time to characterize pain or another chief complaint.
Not this: Airway decisions come from the primary assessment findings, not from a symptom history mnemonic.
Not this: Scene safety is judged during size-up, before any history questions are asked.
Not this: GCS is a separate scored tool for eye, verbal and motor responses, not a pain history.
10: Not this: Fifteen minutes is the usual interval for a stable patient and is too long for an unstable one.
Not this: One check at the start of transport would miss any deterioration that happens on the way.
Correct: Unstable patients can change quickly, so they are reassessed about every 5 minutes.
Not this: Many unstable patients cannot report that they are getting worse, so you cannot wait to be asked.
11: Not this: Scene size-up always comes first, since no exam happens until the scene is known to be safe.
Correct: The more thorough head-to-toe exam is lower priority and is done during transport if time and the patient's condition allow.
Not this: It never replaces the primary assessment, because untreated airway, breathing or circulation problems kill first.
Not this: A patient refusing all care is handled through the refusal process, not with a further hands-on exam.
12: Not this: A minor laceration with bleeding controlled is a stable, low priority injury.
Not this: A patient well enough to ask to walk is showing signs of stability.
Correct: Altered mental status with poor perfusion suggests shock or brain injury, which needs rapid transport and not time on scene.
Not this: An isolated closed forearm fracture with normal mental status can be splinted and transported without urgency.
13: Correct: Facing the patient, asking how they prefer to communicate and using notes or an interpreter gives the most accurate history.
Not this: Speaking loudly assumes one kind of hearing loss and can distort lip patterns, so it often does not help.
Not this: Routing everything through family bypasses the patient and risks missing or distorting the history.
Not this: Hearing loss says nothing about the ability to understand language, so this assumption is unfounded and disrespectful.
14: Not this: A routine blood pressure on a calm patient carries no splash risk.
Not this: Interviewing from a distance involves no body fluid exposure.
Not this: A dry, closed wound will not splash, so gloves are enough.
Correct: Active vomiting or spurting arterial blood can splash the eyes, so eye protection is added to gloves.
15: Not this: A BVM is for inadequate ventilation, and this patient is breathing adequately.
Correct: A hypoxic patient who is ventilating adequately gets oxygen by cannula, titrated up to a saturation of 94 to 98 percent.
Not this: A saturation of 88 percent is hypoxia and is too low to leave untreated.
Not this: A non-rebreather at 15 LPM suits severe distress or carbon monoxide exposure, and is stepped up to only if the cannula fails.
16: Not this: Mild wheezing at a rate of 20 shows air is still moving adequately; this patient needs oxygen as indicated and monitoring, not a BVM.
Not this: A productive cough with a normal rate suggests infection or irritation, but ventilation is still adequate without assistance.
Not this: A rate of 18 with good, consistent tidal volume is the description of adequate breathing, so no assisted ventilation is needed.
Correct: A rate of 6 with shallow, irregular breaths moves too little air each minute, so the patient needs BVM ventilation, not just oxygen.
17: Not this: One breath every 3 to 5 seconds is too fast for an adult and belongs to older child and infant teaching.
Not this: Bagging as fast as possible inflates the stomach, raises chest pressure and reduces blood return to the heart.
Not this: About 6 breaths per minute is too slow and would under-ventilate an apneic adult.
Correct: An apneic adult without an advanced airway gets one breath every 6 seconds, about 10 per minute, each over one second.
18: Not this: A rate of 22 with normal depth and no distress is only mildly elevated and does not point toward failure.
Correct: Diminished or absent breath sounds with visible fatigue mean the muscles are tiring and air movement is dropping, the pattern that precedes respiratory arrest.
Not this: Loud wheezing is alarming but shows air is still moving through narrowed airways, an earlier stage than a quiet, tired chest.
Not this: Mild nasal flaring with otherwise normal effort is an early, mild sign of distress, not impending failure.
19: Not this: Nothing ties cherry-red skin to mild poisoning; when seen at all it is usually in severe or fatal cases.
Not this: It does not appear right away; headache, nausea and confusion come first.
Correct: Cherry-red skin is rare and late, so it cannot be used to confirm or rule out carbon monoxide poisoning.
Not this: Most poisoned patients never show it, so it is neither common nor diagnostic.
20: Not this: Back blows alone leave out the abdominal thrusts that follow if the blows fail.
Correct: Current AHA guidance is cycles of 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts until relief or unresponsiveness.
Not this: Lying flat and waiting lets a complete obstruction progress to hypoxic cardiac arrest.
Not this: Needle cricothyrotomy is far outside EMT scope and is never done on personal judgment.
21: Correct: Forceful coughing and speech show air is moving, so encourage coughing and watch closely.
Not this: A patient with complete obstruction cannot speak or cough forcefully.
Not this: Coughing means something is irritating or partly blocking the airway, so it is not clear.
Not this: Thrusts on a patient with an effective cough can turn a partial obstruction into a complete one.
22: Not this: An apneic patient being bagged has no gag reflex and benefits from an oral airway.
Not this: Unresponsive with no gag reflex is exactly the indication for an oral airway.
Not this: Cardiac arrest patients have no gag reflex, and an oral airway helps ventilation.
Correct: An intact gag reflex means the oral airway will cause gagging, vomiting and aspiration.
23: Not this: An unresponsive patient without facial trauma is a suitable candidate for a nasal airway.
Not this: An apneic patient needs an adjunct to help ventilation, so this is an indication.
Not this: An intact gag reflex is the reason to choose a nasal airway over an oral one.
Correct: With severe facial or skull base fracture the tube could pass through the fracture toward the brain.
24: Not this: Suction removes air and stops ventilation, so every pass must be timed.
Correct: Adult suction passes are limited to about 15 seconds to avoid causing hypoxia.
Not this: Sixty seconds of continuous suction would cause serious desaturation.
Not this: Suctioning until clear without a limit risks hypoxia, so you oxygenate between passes.
25: Not this: The bag can empty through a mask leak or into the stomach without any air reaching the lungs.
Not this: Gurgling means fluid in the airway that needs suction, not effective ventilation.
Correct: Seeing the chest rise with each breath confirms air is entering the lungs in adequate volume.
Not this: Color does matter; cyanosis that persists during bagging means oxygenation is still inadequate.
26: Correct: Sitting upright or tripoding lets the diaphragm drop and the accessory muscles work, so breathing takes the least effort.
Not this: Trendelenburg pushes the abdominal contents up against the diaphragm and makes a distressed breather work harder.
Not this: Left lateral recumbent suits late pregnancy or an unresponsive patient who may vomit, not an alert patient fighting to breathe.
Not this: Lying supine with legs raised is an old shock position and worsens the work of breathing in asthma.
27: Not this: A nosebleed does not change how hemoglobin absorbs the oximeter's light.
Not this: A twisted ankle has no effect on an oximeter reading taken at a finger.
Correct: Carbon monoxide bound to hemoglobin is read by a standard oximeter as oxygen, so the number looks normal while tissues starve.
Not this: Mild anxiety with normal breathing does not interfere with the oximeter.
28: Not this: Looking in the mouth with a tongue depressor can trigger spasm and complete obstruction.
Correct: The upright, forward lean keeps the swollen airway open, and calm prevents sudden obstruction.
Not this: Lying supine lets the swollen epiglottis fall back and close the airway.
Not this: Forcing the child flat causes agitation and can close the airway completely.
29: Not this: Mild dyspnea with equal breath sounds and stable vitals does not fit air building under pressure in one side of the chest.
Not this: A rate of 16 with unlabored breathing is normal and gives no sign of a developing tension pneumothorax.
Not this: A small superficial laceration without bruising or breathing changes suggests no injury to the pleura or lung.
Correct: Worsening distress, absent breath sounds on one side and tracheal deviation show trapped air collapsing the lung and shifting the mediastinum.
30: Not this: Kussmaul breathing, dehydration and gradual onset describe DKA from high sugar, the opposite end of the diabetic spectrum.
Correct: Low sugar hits within minutes and triggers an adrenaline response, giving cool clammy skin, confusion and sometimes combativeness.
Not this: Slow pulse, high pressure and flushed skin fit neither diabetic emergency and point to another problem such as raised intracranial pressure.
Not this: Slow onset, warm dry skin, fruity breath and deep rapid breathing are the classic DKA picture, not low sugar.
31: Not this: Neurons take up glucose without insulin, and blood sugar is very high in DKA, so the brain is not starved of fuel.
Not this: Potassium shifts happen in DKA and threaten the heart rhythm, but they are not the main reason the patient is confused.
Correct: Very high sugar pulls water out of cells, and the dehydration plus ketone acidosis together impair how the brain works.
Not this: DKA comes from too little insulin, not too much, so excess insulin cannot be the mechanism here.
32: Not this: Recent food intake does not affect nitroglycerin safety; the drug's danger is a drop in blood pressure.
Correct: Nitroglycerin dilates vessels and can drop pressure, so systolic must meet the protocol minimum of 100 before each dose.
Not this: Glucose is checked for altered mental status, not as a safety check before assisting with nitroglycerin.
Not this: Respiratory rate matters for assessment but is not a nitroglycerin contraindication check; blood pressure is.
33: Not this: Pupils, grip and gait can be part of a neuro exam, but none of them is a Cincinnati scale item.
Not this: Headache, nausea and vomiting may accompany a hemorrhagic stroke but they are symptoms, not the three Cincinnati tests.
Correct: The Cincinnati scale checks facial droop, arm drift and speech, and any one abnormal finding is a positive screen.
Not this: Vital signs are taken on every stroke patient but they are not part of the Cincinnati stroke screen.
34: Not this: Itching only at the exposure site with no rash or swelling is a mild local reaction that is simply monitored.
Not this: One sneeze with no skin or breathing changes involves no body system seriously and is not anaphylaxis.
Correct: Hives all over plus breathing trouble or low blood pressure means a systemic reaction, which is the indication for epinephrine.
Not this: Hives that stay at the exposure site with no systemic signs are a local reaction and do not need epinephrine.
35: Not this: 140 to 160 per minute at 3 inches is too fast and too deep, reducing filling and causing injury.
Not this: Rate and depth both matter; compressions that are too slow or too fast move less blood.
Correct: Adult compressions are 100 to 120 per minute at a depth of at least 2 inches, avoiding excessive depth.
Not this: 60 to 80 per minute at 1 inch is far too slow and shallow to circulate blood.
36: Not this: 5:1 is an outdated ratio and is not used in current adult CPR.
Not this: Compression-only CPR is for untrained lay rescuers; an EMT gives breaths with a barrier device or BVM.
Not this: 15:2 is for two rescuers on a child or infant, not single-rescuer adult CPR.
Correct: Adult CPR without an advanced airway uses 30 compressions to 2 breaths, whether one rescuer or two.
37: Not this: Touching the patient for a pulse check during analysis creates artifact and delays the AED.
Not this: Ventilating moves the chest and can corrupt the rhythm analysis; hands and BVM come off.
Correct: Nobody touches the patient during analysis, because movement and contact cause artifact and a wrong shock decision.
Not this: Compressions during analysis create motion artifact; they resume immediately after the shock or no-shock message.
38: Not this: Pain identical to many earlier episodes with the same resolution is the predictable pattern of stable angina.
Correct: Pain that continues despite rest and prescribed nitroglycerin suggests ongoing blockage and infarction, not reversible angina.
Not this: Exertional pain that eases within minutes of stopping is classic stable angina.
Not this: Complete relief with a few minutes of rest points to stable angina rather than infarction.
39: Not this: The time is documented, but its real value is deciding treatment eligibility, not satisfying paperwork after the call.
Not this: Bed availability is a hospital logistics matter and has nothing to do with when the patient was last normal.
Correct: Clot dissolving drugs and clot retrieval are only offered within set windows counted from the last known well time.
Not this: Visiting hours have no connection to stroke care; this option is a distractor with no clinical meaning.
40: Correct: Confusion and drowsiness that slowly clear after a generalized seizure are the expected postictal recovery phase.
Not this: Postictal confusion follows any generalized seizure and says nothing about fever; that needs age and temperature history.
Not this: An ongoing seizure shows continued convulsions or no improvement at all, while this patient is recovering after it ended.
Not this: Postictal confusion is far more likely than stroke here; stroke is considered only if focal deficits persist.
41: Not this: Holding the limbs down does not stop a seizure and can cause fractures or dislocations.
Correct: Clear hazards and cushion the head during the seizure, then manage the airway as soon as the convulsions stop.
Not this: Forcing anything between clenched teeth breaks teeth, injures the airway and risks the rescuer's fingers.
Not this: A seizing patient cannot swallow safely, so food or water would be aspirated.
42: Not this: Corrosives are a contraindication, since charcoal does not bind them and may cause vomiting.
Correct: Charcoal binds certain poisons still in the gut, so it works best early and only under protocol.
Not this: After several hours most of the poison has been absorbed and charcoal adds little.
Not this: Charcoal does not bind every substance and has no role for inhaled or absorbed poisons.
43: Correct: Abnormal temperature, altered mental status and poor perfusion in an infected patient suggest the infection has become systemic.
Not this: Normal vitals and baseline alertness are reassuring and show no sign of a systemic response to infection.
Not this: A healed scar with no redness or drainage shows no active infection at all, let alone sepsis.
Not this: One sneeze with a normal exam is trivial and involves none of the perfusion or mental status changes of sepsis.
44: Not this: Finding the exact cause needs labs, imaging and surgical exams that are outside EMT scope and would delay care.
Not this: Waiting on scene for a diagnosis delays the hospital evaluation that a serious abdominal problem needs.
Correct: The EMT takes a history, looks for red flags such as shock or a rigid abdomen, and transports promptly.
Not this: Abdominal pain patients are kept without food or drink because of vomiting, aspiration and possible surgery.
45: Not this: A loud commanding voice feels threatening to an agitated patient and usually escalates the situation.
Not this: Telling the patient their concerns are not serious dismisses them, damages rapport and increases agitation.
Correct: A calm voice, safe distance and slow movements are de-escalation steps that lower perceived threat and protect the crew.
Not this: Restraint is a last resort for a patient who is a danger, not a precaution for one who is only agitated.
47: Not this: Discomfort is not the reason; the real concern is damaging or clotting the dialysis access.
Correct: Cuff pressure can clot or damage the fistula, and losing that access can delay life sustaining dialysis.
Not this: The effect on the reading is unpredictable, and accuracy is not the reason the arm is avoided.
Not this: Whether sounds can be heard is beside the point; the arm is avoided to protect the access.
48: Not this: An allergic reaction brings hives, swelling or wheezing, not severe bone and joint pain in a sickle cell patient.
Not this: Severe pain in sickle cell disease is never routine and can precede acute chest syndrome or stroke.
Correct: Sickled cells block small vessels in bones and joints, causing the ischemic pain of a vaso-occlusive crisis.
Not this: A strain follows a specific injury and stays local; diffuse bone and joint pain in sickle cell disease is a crisis.
49: Not this: Paper bag rebreathing is no longer taught because it is dangerous if the real cause is hypoxia or acidosis.
Not this: Anxiety is a real condition, and these symptoms can also come from serious illness, so they are never ignored.
Correct: Hyperventilation from anxiety is a diagnosis of exclusion, so embolism, DKA, cardiac and other causes are assessed for first.
Not this: Oxygen decisions follow assessment and SpO2; assuming anxiety and withholding it could harm a hypoxic patient.
50: Not this: Pressure points are no longer emphasized because they do not reliably control severe bleeding.
Not this: A loose bandage gives no compression and will not slow a life threatening hemorrhage.
Not this: Elevation without direct pressure has no proven benefit and wastes time in severe bleeding.
Correct: Firm direct pressure with early tourniquet use is the current standard for life threatening extremity bleeding.
51: Not this: Assessment cannot wait; life threats must be found before and during transport.
Not this: A head-only exam misses chest, abdominal, pelvic and spinal injuries from a 15 foot fall.
Correct: A significant mechanism plus altered mental status calls for a rapid head-to-toe trauma assessment.
Not this: A focused exam suits a minor isolated injury in a reliable patient, not an altered patient after a high fall.
52: Not this: Head tilt extends the neck and is avoided unless the jaw thrust fails to open the airway.
Not this: Cricoid pressure does not open the airway and is no longer routinely recommended.
Not this: An unopened airway kills; airway always takes priority over the spine.
Correct: The jaw thrust moves the mandible forward and opens the airway without extending the neck.
53: Correct: A free segment from ribs broken in two or more places moves inward on inspiration and outward on expiration.
Not this: Sternal bruising without instability suggests a chest wall contusion, not a free floating rib segment.
Not this: Crepitus in the neck suggests subcutaneous air from an airway or lung leak, not a flail segment.
Not this: Absent breath sounds on one side point to a pneumothorax or hemothorax rather than a flail segment.
54: Not this: Loss of radial pulses with a weak carotid pulse is a late finding of decompensated shock.
Not this: Clear hypotension means compensation has already failed, which is a late sign.
Correct: A fast heart rate with blood pressure still normal or nearly normal shows the body compensating, which is early shock.
Not this: Unresponsiveness with agonal breathing is a pre arrest finding at the very end of shock.
55: Not this: Direct contact with ice freezes the tissue and can make reattachment impossible.
Not this: Replantation is often attempted and can succeed, so the part always travels with the patient.
Not this: Soaking the bare part in saline waterlogs and damages the tissue.
Correct: A sterile dressing, a sealed plastic bag and ice under the bag keep the part clean and cool without freezing it.
56: Correct: The object is stabilized in place with bulky dressings because it may be plugging a vessel, and removal is left to surgeons.
Not this: Pushing the object deeper causes new damage to vessels and organs.
Not this: Twisting or moving the object tears tissue and can restart or worsen bleeding.
Not this: Pulling it out in the field can release severe bleeding that cannot be controlled outside surgery.
58: Correct: A moist sterile dressing keeps exposed bowel from drying, and organs are never pushed back in the field.
Not this: A tourniquet works only on limbs and cannot compress the abdomen or control bleeding from organs.
Not this: Leaving the organs uncovered lets them dry, cool and become contaminated, which kills tissue.
Not this: Replacing the organs carries contamination into the abdomen and can injure bowel, so it is left to surgeons.
59: Not this: 4.5 percent is only the front or the back of one arm, not the whole arm.
Not this: 36 percent is the whole trunk, front and back together.
Not this: 18 percent is one whole leg or one side of the trunk in an adult.
Correct: One entire arm, front and back, counts as 9 percent in the adult rule of nines.
60: Correct: Cool water stops heat from continuing to damage the tissue and eases the pain.
Not this: Cooling narrows vessels and does not work by increasing blood flow or flushing tissue.
Not this: Whole body immersion in ice water causes hypothermia and further tissue injury.
Not this: Waiting for the hospital gives up the early minutes when cooling does the most good.
61: Not this: A scalp laceration bleeds heavily but does not raise blood pressure, slow the heart or disturb breathing.
Not this: Hypovolemic shock produces a fast pulse and falling blood pressure, the opposite of this pattern.
Correct: High pressure, slow pulse and irregular breathing together are a late sign of rising intracranial pressure and possible herniation.
Not this: Cushing's triad signals a deteriorating brain, so this patient is unstable and getting worse.
62: Correct: Current guidance applies spinal motion restriction selectively using assessment criteria instead of backboarding everyone.
Not this: Routine backboarding of every trauma patient is outdated and causes pain, pressure injury and breathing restriction.
Not this: Pain is only one criterion; altered mental status, intoxication, deficits and distracting injuries also count.
Not this: Mechanism alone no longer decides; the patient's examination findings do.
63: Not this: A binder slows the bleeding but does not replace lost volume, so shock care is still needed.
Correct: The binder compresses and stabilizes the pelvic ring, which limits bone movement and reduces internal bleeding.
Not this: Securing the legs is not the purpose; the goal is closing the pelvic ring to limit bleeding.
Not this: Comfort is a side benefit, and the binder does meaningfully reduce bleeding.
64: Not this: A head-to-toe exam does not come before treating the causes of a traumatic arrest.
Not this: Withholding CPR and all care until hospital removes any chance of survival.
Not this: History taking never precedes hands-on care in a pulseless patient.
Correct: Traumatic arrest often has a reversible cause, so hemorrhage control and relief of tension pneumothorax are urgent priorities.
65: Correct: Singed nasal hair, soot around the mouth or nose, and a hoarse voice show that hot gas or smoke reached the airway.
Not this: A superficial burn limited to one hand is far from the airway and involved no inhalation.
Not this: A calm patient with a normal voice shows no current airway signs, though you keep watching.
Not this: A burn in open, ventilated air makes smoke inhalation much less likely than a fire in an enclosed space.
66: Not this: Nerve compression causes numbness, but crush syndrome is the systemic effect of muscle breakdown.
Not this: Crush syndrome is defined by its systemic effects on the heart and kidneys.
Not this: Bone healing is a late orthopedic matter, not the danger of crush syndrome.
Correct: Released muscle breakdown products, especially potassium and myoglobin, cause dysrhythmias and kidney injury.
67: Not this: A tooth out for minutes can still be reimplanted, so it is preserved and transported with the patient.
Not this: Drying kills the ligament cells on the root within minutes and ruins the chance of reimplantation.
Correct: Holding the crown protects the root cells, and milk or saline keeps them alive for reimplantation.
Not this: Scrubbing with soap strips and kills the root surface cells needed for the tooth to reattach.
68: Not this: Routine hyperventilation is no longer recommended for brain injury because it reduces blood flow to the brain.
Correct: Blowing off carbon dioxide narrows cerebral vessels and cuts blood flow to an already injured brain.
Not this: Ventilation rate directly changes carbon dioxide, which controls cerebral vessel diameter and so blood flow and pressure.
Not this: Extra breaths add little oxygen, and the loss of cerebral blood flow outweighs any gain.
69: Not this: A mild ache that goes away with rest and elevation is reassuring and not typical of compartment syndrome.
Not this: Slight bruising with no pain or swelling does not suggest rising pressure in a compartment.
Correct: Pain far worse than the injury looks, especially on passive stretch, is the earliest reliable sign of compartment syndrome.
Not this: Warm skin, strong pulses and no complaints describe a well perfused limb.
70: Not this: A rate of 200 to 220 is abnormally fast even for a newborn and should raise concern, not be accepted as normal.
Correct: A healthy newborn runs roughly 100 to 180 beats per minute, usually about 120 to 160, far faster than an adult.
Not this: A rate of 40 to 60 is normal for a resting adult but is severe bradycardia in a newborn and needs immediate action.
Not this: A rate of 80 to 100 is below the 100 threshold, so in a newborn it is slow and signals a need for ventilation.
71: Not this: Pain response and gestational age are not APGAR components. The P is pulse and the G is grimace.
Not this: Apnea, gag reflex and alertness are not what the letters stand for, even though pulse does appear in the real score.
Correct: APGAR stands for Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity and Respirations, each scored 0 to 2.
Not this: Airway and glucose are not scored in APGAR. The A is appearance (skin color) and the G is grimace.
72: Not this: Intubation is an advanced step far down the algorithm and outside EMT scope. Most newborns respond to drying and stimulation.
Correct: The first steps are to dry, warm, stimulate and position or clear the airway, then reassess breathing before escalating.
Not this: Compressions come only if the heart rate stays below 60 despite effective ventilation, never before the initial steps and assessment.
Not this: Many newborns breathe well once dried and stimulated, so ventilating every baby before assessing is unnecessary.
73: Correct: The triangle is appearance, work of breathing and circulation to skin, all judged by looking and listening from across the room.
Not this: SAMPLE, OPQRST and baseline vitals need questions, hands and equipment, so they come after the across the room impression.
Not this: Weight, age and immunization status are history details gathered later and tell you nothing about how sick the child looks now.
Not this: Blood pressure, pulse and respirations are measured vital signs that require touching the child, which the triangle deliberately avoids.
74: Not this: Slower rates describe the opposite of pediatric physiology, where small stroke and tidal volumes are offset by faster rates.
Not this: Rates run fast from birth and drift toward adult values with age, so nothing special begins after age 12.
Not this: School age children still have faster normal heart and breathing rates than adults, so adult norms cannot be applied.
Correct: Higher metabolic demand with smaller stroke and tidal volumes means healthy children run faster heart and respiratory rates than adults.
75: Correct: A narrow airway, a relatively large tongue and a higher, more anterior larynx make a child's airway easier to obstruct.
Not this: The pediatric airway is narrower, not larger, so a little swelling or mucus blocks proportionally more of it.
Not this: It is not just a scaled down adult airway, because the tongue, larynx position and narrowest point all differ.
Not this: A child's airway cartilage is softer and more pliable, so it kinks and collapses rather than fracturing.
76: Not this: Febrile seizures are a problem of the young developing brain and do not occur in adults with chronic fevers.
Not this: Most febrile seizures are brief and self limited, and most children never need long term anticonvulsant therapy.
Not this: The definition depends on fever, so a seizure unrelated to temperature or illness is by definition something else.
Correct: A febrile seizure is triggered by fever, typically a rapid rise, in children roughly 6 months to 5 years old.
77: Not this: A clear, consistent history that fits the injury is reassuring and is what a true accident usually looks like.
Not this: Shin bruises on a toddler learning to walk are expected accidental injuries over a bony prominence.
Correct: A vague or changing story that does not fit the injury, or an injury the infant could not cause developmentally, is a red flag.
Not this: Normal behavior and development with no injury gives no reason to suspect abusive head trauma.
78: Not this: Back strain is a comfort issue. The real danger of lying supine is reduced blood return to the heart.
Not this: Supine positioning does affect the mother's circulation. The uterus presses on the vena cava and blood pressure can fall.
Not this: Lying flat has a real effect. The heavy uterus compresses the inferior vena cava and lowers cardiac output.
Correct: The uterus can compress the inferior vena cava when she lies supine, cutting venous return and causing hypotension.
79: Not this: Pushing the cord back in does not relieve compression and can injure it or introduce infection.
Not this: Pulling on the cord can tear it or injure the baby and placenta, and it does nothing for the compression.
Not this: A prolapsed cord will not fix itself. The baby can lose its oxygen supply within minutes, so this is an emergency.
Correct: Positioning the mother to take pressure off the cord, keeping it moist and transporting at once protects the baby's oxygen supply.
80: Correct: Older adults having an MI often present with shortness of breath, fatigue or confusion and little or no chest pain.
Not this: Classic crushing chest pain in essentially every case is not true of older adults, who often have none.
Not this: Older patients frequently do not mirror the classic presentation seen in younger adults.
Not this: Brief discomfort that clears in seconds does not describe an MI at any age.
81: Not this: One bruise that matches a witnessed fall has a consistent, believable explanation.
Not this: A clean home with fresh food and properly stored medications suggests good care.
Not this: An alert patient who reports no concerns in private is reassuring.
Correct: Injuries in different healing stages, poor hygiene, and a caregiver who blocks private conversation are recognized warning signs of abuse or neglect.
82: Correct: Reducing lights, noise and touch, using plain concrete language, and allowing extra time lowers distress and improves cooperation.
Not this: Immediate restraint is frightening, escalates distress, and is not justified by a diagnosis alone.
Not this: Many autistic patients understand well even when they speak little, so the patient is still addressed directly.
Not this: A loud voice and rapid complex speech overload the senses and increase distress.
83: Not this: Standard stretchers and two person crews may be over their limits, so planning must differ.
Correct: Calling early for a bariatric stretcher and extra personnel prevents equipment failure and injury to patient and crew.
Not this: Assuming standard equipment will do risks a stretcher failure or a dropped patient.
Not this: Lifesaving care for an unstable patient is never delayed while waiting for lifting help.
84: Not this: A bulging, tense fontanelle points to raised intracranial pressure, and tearing with high urine output shows good hydration.
Not this: Frequent wet diapers with pale urine show the kidneys are well perfused, which is the opposite of dehydration.
Not this: Moist membranes, good turgor and normal behavior are the reassuring findings you hope to see in a hydrated infant.
Correct: A sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes and fewer wet diapers together are the classic picture of significant infant dehydration.
85: Not this: Hazard lights alone do not create a physical barrier or give drivers enough warning.
Not this: Parking as close as possible ignores traffic flow and can leave the crew working in the path of vehicles.
Correct: Position the ambulance to protect the scene from traffic, with warning lights on and cones out.
Not this: Blocking every lane at every crash is not standard and can cause secondary collisions from sudden backups.
86: Correct: The first unit sizes up the scene, establishes command and calls for resources so the whole response is organized.
Not this: Size up, command and triage start on arrival and cannot wait for other units.
Not this: Committing to one patient leaves the other patients and the scene unmanaged.
Not this: Leaving with one patient abandons the scene before anyone knows how many others need help.
87: Not this: START uses four categories, not just alive and dead.
Not this: Age alone does not set priority; START sorts by physiological findings.
Not this: Order of discovery ignores severity, so quiet critical patients would be missed.
Correct: START sorts into Immediate, Delayed, Minor and Deceased using walking, breathing, perfusion and mental status.
88: Not this: Self extrication before any assessment risks worsening injuries in a patient who has not been checked.
Correct: Once it is safe, reach the patient and start critical care such as airway and bleeding control while extrication continues.
Not this: Life threats cannot wait for the doors. Access through any safe opening lets care begin.
Not this: Waiting until the patient is out leaves airway and bleeding problems untreated during a long extrication.
89: Correct: At a suspected hazmat release, stage at a safe distance and request specialized resources before any approach.
Not this: Approaching before the hazard is confirmed can make you a second victim.
Not this: Many hazardous materials have no odor or color, and getting close enough to smell them can be lethal.
Not this: Entering quickly exposes the crew. A delay is safer than adding responders to the casualty count.
90: Correct: Trouble sleeping, irritability and intrusive thoughts are common, normal reactions in the days after a hard call.
Not this: Symptoms still disrupting work after a month suggest post-traumatic stress disorder and need professional help.
Not this: Drinking heavily to sleep is harmful coping and a warning sign, not a normal acute reaction.
Not this: Thoughts of self-harm are never a normal stress reaction and need immediate professional help.
91: Correct: The PCR is the legal and medical record of the assessment, care given and patient response.
Not this: The written report follows the verbal handoff and never replaces it.
Not this: A PCR is completed for every patient contact, including refusals and other calls without transport.
Not this: The report supports billing, but that is a secondary use and not its main purpose.
92: Not this: A verbal no alone does not show the refusal was informed, which is why the risk discussion is documented and signed.
Not this: A family member cannot co-decide for a competent adult, so their signature is not required.
Not this: A police signature does not make a refusal valid; capacity and informed understanding do.
Correct: A valid refusal needs legal age or emancipation, mental competence and an understanding of the risks explained.
93: Not this: A responsive, competent adult must give expressed consent, so implied consent does not cover every contact.
Correct: Implied consent assumes an unresponsive or incapacitated patient would want life-saving care if able to say so.
Not this: No form is involved; implied consent exists precisely because the patient cannot sign or agree.
Not this: It is not limited to children; minors are covered by a related doctrine when no parent can be reached.
94: Not this: Declining a new call while caring for a patient keeps your existing duty and abandons no one.
Not this: Handing off to emergency department staff transfers care to equal or higher training, which is proper.
Not this: Honoring a valid informed refusal respects the patient's choice and breaches no duty.
Correct: Abandonment is ending care without the patient's consent and without handing off to an equal or higher level provider.
95: Not this: EMS providers have no blanket immunity and can be held liable for negligence.
Not this: Unhappiness alone proves nothing if the care met the standard and caused no harm.
Not this: A deviation without resulting harm lacks the damages and causation elements.
Correct: Negligence needs all four: a duty to act, a breach, damages, and causation linking the two.
96: Not this: Plain language is the standard for tactical radio traffic, not just for public announcements.
Not this: The benefit is in real time coordination between agencies, not only in later documentation.
Not this: Codes are not consistent between agencies, which is the problem plain language solves.
Correct: The same code can mean different things to different agencies, so plain language avoids dangerous confusion.
97: Not this: Size and surface matter. A small, sloped or cluttered site puts the aircraft and people on the ground at risk.
Not this: The landing zone is chosen for safety, not closeness. The patient is brought to it if needed.
Correct: A landing zone must be large enough, fairly flat and free of obstructions, with bystanders and loose objects kept clear.
Not this: Every landing needs ground coordination and a hazard check, because pilots cannot see wires and debris.
98: Not this: A police all clear is not permanent. A suspect can return or tempers can flare again.
Not this: Interviewing in front of the suspected abuser suppresses disclosure and can provoke more violence.
Correct: Domestic violence scenes can turn volatile again at any time, so stay alert throughout the call.
Not this: Police involvement depends on scene safety and reporting laws, not only on the patient's request.
99: Not this: Family do not receive information by default; a competent patient decides who is told.
Correct: Information goes only to those involved in the patient's care or to parties the law requires or authorizes.
Not this: An interesting call is never a legal or ethical reason to share patient information.
Not this: Sharing with anyone who asks or on social media violates confidentiality regardless of intent.
100: Correct: The GCS scores best eye opening, best verbal response and best motor response for a total of 3 to 15.
Not this: Pupil checks are a separate neurological exam often done alongside the GCS but are not scored in it.
Not this: Pulse, respirations and blood pressure are vital signs and are recorded apart from the GCS.
Not this: Skin color, temperature and moisture are perfusion signs and are not GCS components.
101: Correct: Fifteen is the maximum: spontaneous eye opening (4), oriented speech (5) and obeying commands (6).
Not this: A total of 15 is the expected finding in a healthy alert person and does not signal an error.
Not this: Deep coma scores at the bottom of the scale, near the minimum of 3, not at 15.
Not this: Complete unresponsiveness earns 1 point per component for a total of 3, the opposite end from 15.
102: Not this: Pain tolerance is subjective and is not what a distal pulse, motor and sensory check measures.
Correct: Injuries can compress or tear nearby nerves and vessels, so the check screens for compromise beyond the injury.
Not this: Splinting is decided by the injury itself; the check is done before and after splinting to catch any change.
Not this: Hospital choice follows the patient's overall condition and protocols, not a distal function check alone.
103: Not this: Breathing effort, rate and depth are assessed by watching and listening, not by these questions.
Not this: Capillary refill is checked by pressing on a nail bed or skin.
Not this: Pain is rated with a separate zero to ten question.
Correct: Name, place, date and event test orientation to person, place, time and event, reported as alert and oriented times four.
104: Not this: The car and ground may be energized, so approaching can electrocute you.
Not this: A wooden pole is not safe insulation, and moving lines is the utility's job.
Correct: Stage at a safe distance until the utility or fire service confirms the line is dead.
Not this: A patient who steps out can be electrocuted. He should stay inside unless fire forces an exit.
105: Not this: A stubbed toe is a trivial isolated injury.
Correct: Ejection from a vehicle is a high energy mechanism with a high risk of hidden injuries to several body systems.
Not this: A standing height fall with no complaints is a low energy mechanism.
Not this: A low speed fender bender with no complaints is a low energy mechanism.
107: Not this: Objective findings still matter greatly and are never set aside for the patient's own guess at a diagnosis.
Not this: Diagnosis names a disease and treatment manages a problem; EMTs do the second without needing the first.
Not this: Naming the exact disease needs labs and imaging EMTs lack, and waiting for it would delay urgent care.
Correct: EMTs treat the functional problem in front of them, such as poor perfusion or inadequate breathing, whatever the final cause.
108: Not this: What the patient denies is clinically useful and belongs in the report.
Not this: A denial of symptoms is history from the patient, not a measured vital sign.
Not this: Mechanism of injury describes how trauma happened and comes from the scene, not from symptom questions.
Correct: Relevant symptoms the patient denies, such as shortness of breath, nausea or radiation, are pertinent negatives.
109: Correct: Compensation can keep one reading acceptable, so the direction of change over repeated sets is what exposes deterioration.
Not this: Vital signs can change meaningfully within one call, which is exactly why they are repeated.
Not this: Trending matters most in sick or injured patients, where a climbing pulse may be the only early warning.
Not this: A single set is only a snapshot and can look normal while the patient is still compensating.
110: Not this: Feeling a pulse tells you nothing about how fast the heart is beating.
Correct: A radial pulse shows some blood is reaching the periphery, but it is a rough sign and not a pressure number.
Not this: A palpable radial pulse argues against a critically low pressure, although it cannot give an exact figure.
Not this: A pulse at the wrist means there is some perfusion, which rules out a pulseless state.
111: Not this: Looking for family is useful, but treatment of what you find should not wait on it.
Correct: Without a history you lean on the exam, scene clues such as pill bottles, and any other available sources.
Not this: Altered mental status always needs a full assessment for treatable causes and is never assumed to be faking.
Not this: Withholding all care until a perfect historian appears leaves a possibly critical patient untreated.
112: Correct: A responsive medical patient can tell you what is wrong, so the history and a focused exam drive the assessment.
Not this: A rapid head-to-toe exam suits trauma or unresponsive patients and wastes time on an alert medical patient.
Not this: Vital signs matter, but skipping the complaint and history discards the richest information this patient offers.
Not this: Looking only where the patient points is too narrow, since related or referred findings can sit elsewhere.
113: Not this: Talking to family helps but cannot replace a hands-on exam of the patient.
Not this: The exam is the main source of objective data here and is not optional, even when bystanders give a history.
Correct: With no complaint to focus on, a rapid full-body exam searches for clues such as medical jewelry, injection sites or injury.
Not this: A single-system exam assumes you know the cause, which is exactly what is missing in this patient.
114: Correct: A collapsed structure can collapse further, so entry waits until trained personnel have assessed it as safe.
Not this: Passive waiting with no communication is wrong. Coordinate with incoming rescue resources.
Not this: Rushing in risks a second collapse and makes you another casualty.
Not this: Screaming does not make the structure any safer to enter.
115: Not this: A rate above 40 is usually too fast to allow adequate tidal volume, so it signals distress rather than good oxygenation.
Not this: Shallow, rapid breaths with retractions describe increased work of breathing and poor tidal volume, which is inadequate breathing.
Correct: Adequate breathing means a normal rate with enough depth, a regular rhythm and equal chest rise so gas exchange is maintained.
Not this: Slow, gasping, irregular breaths with long pauses are agonal respirations, a peri-arrest pattern that needs ventilation.
116: Not this: Retractions mean the child is struggling to move air, so oxygenation and ventilation are threatened, not assured.
Not this: Swallowed air causes gastric distention, which shows as a swollen abdomen, not skin pulling in between the ribs.
Not this: Effortless breathing has no retractions; pulling in at the ribs and neck is accessory muscle use by definition.
Correct: Retractions show the child is using accessory muscles against resistance, a reliable sign of increased work of breathing and significant distress.
117: Correct: Stridor is turbulent airflow through a narrowed larynx or trachea, an upper airway emergency.
Not this: Fluid in the lower lungs causes crackles, not a high pitched inspiratory sound.
Not this: Stridor is never normal and always signals airway narrowing.
Not this: Asthma narrows the small lower airways and causes wheezing, mainly on exhalation.
118: Correct: Crackles come from air passing through fluid filled or reopening alveoli, as in pulmonary edema and pneumonia.
Not this: A pneumothorax gives diminished or absent breath sounds on the affected side, not crackles.
Not this: Upper airway obstruction produces stridor; crackles arise in the small lower airways and alveoli.
Not this: Clear, healthy lungs have no added sounds, and crackles are an abnormal added sound.
119: Not this: A patient in cardiac arrest is not moving air, so there is no airflow to produce a wheeze.
Not this: Wheezing is an abnormal added lung sound and is never an expected finding in a healthy patient at rest.
Not this: A foreign body in the upper airway typically causes stridor, a harsh high pitched sound heard on inspiration.
Correct: Wheezing is the whistling of air forced through narrowed bronchioles, the mechanism in asthma and COPD.
120: Not this: Conserving the tank is never a reason to under-treat hypoxia, and a low flow lets the reservoir bag collapse.
Correct: A non-rebreather needs 10 to 15 LPM so the reservoir bag stays inflated and the patient breathes high concentration oxygen.
Not this: At 1 to 2 LPM the bag collapses and the patient rebreathes exhaled air; that flow belongs to a cannula.
Not this: A fixed 6 LPM is too low to keep the reservoir bag inflated through each breath.
121: Correct: A nasal cannula is a low-flow device run at 1 to 6 LPM, delivering roughly 24 to 44 percent oxygen.
Not this: Flows up to 15 LPM dry and irritate the nose and add little; that range is for a non-rebreather.
Not this: A standard cannula cannot be run at 25 LPM; that needs special heated high-flow equipment.
Not this: 15 LPM is the non-rebreather flow, far above the cannula's range.
122: Not this: A pulseless, apneic patient has no breathing for CPAP to support and needs CPR and BVM ventilation.
Not this: A complete obstruction must be cleared with obstruction maneuvers; CPAP cannot relieve a blockage.
Not this: Mild shortness of breath with normal saturation and no distress does not meet the threshold for CPAP.
Correct: CPAP suits an alert patient in moderate to severe distress who is still breathing well enough to cooperate with the mask.
123: Not this: An alert patient in distress who protects the airway is the ideal CPAP candidate.
Not this: A request without distress is not an indication, though it is not the classic contraindication being tested.
Not this: Mild symptoms without distress simply do not need CPAP; that is lack of indication, not a contraindication.
Correct: A patient with decreased consciousness cannot protect the airway, and positive pressure can turn a pneumothorax into tension.
124: Correct: One rescuer holds the seal and airway position with two hands while the other squeezes, so more of each breath reaches the lungs.
Not this: Oxygen use depends on flow and rate, not on how many rescuers hold the equipment.
Not this: Head tilt or jaw thrust is still required; bagging does not hold an airway open.
Not this: No law requires two rescuers; it is preferred because it works better.
125: Not this: Better color and rising saturation are signs the ventilations are working.
Not this: A steady, appropriate rate with a good seal describes proper technique.
Correct: No chest rise and no improvement in saturation mean air is not reaching the lungs, so position, seal and airway must be rechecked.
Not this: Equal, visible chest rise with each squeeze is the best sign of effective ventilation.
126: Not this: Over-ventilation carries real harm and no guarantee of better oxygenation.
Correct: Too much volume or speed forces air into the stomach, which leads to vomiting and aspiration.
Not this: Bagging supports the patient but does not treat the underlying cause.
Not this: Over-ventilation distends the stomach and raises chest pressure, lowering blood return to the heart.
127: Not this: Lying on the side does not raise blood pressure.
Not this: Compressions need a supine patient on a firm surface, and this patient is breathing.
Not this: The recovery position is avoided when spinal injury is suspected, so it is not preparation for immobilization.
Correct: On the side, vomit and secretions drain out of the mouth instead of into the lungs.
128: Not this: Maximum flow for every COPD patient ignores titration; the goal is to correct hypoxia, not to give as much as possible.
Correct: Oxygen is titrated to correct hypoxia while the EMT watches mental status and breathing effort for any decline.
Not this: Withholding oxygen from a hypoxic COPD patient is dangerous; untreated hypoxia harms far sooner than any blunting of respiratory drive.
Not this: Oxygen decisions rest on saturation and clinical findings; a hypoxic patient may not report feeling short of breath.
129: Not this: Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper and are not used at any age.
Not this: Abdominal thrusts can injure an infant's liver and are not used under one year.
Not this: Waiting for unresponsiveness wastes the time when the obstruction is most easily relieved.
Correct: Infants receive cycles of 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until the object clears.
130: Correct: The chain runs from early recognition and activation through CPR, defibrillation and advanced care to post-arrest care.
Not this: Two-minute compression cycles are one piece of CPR; ignoring defibrillation and advanced care breaks the chain.
Not this: Help is called at once on recognizing arrest; delaying activation delays the defibrillator and advanced care.
Not this: Defibrillation works best with early recognition and CPR keeping the heart perfused; every link matters.
131: Not this: Applying AED pads is an intervention and says nothing about whether a pulse has returned.
Correct: ROSC means the heart has resumed organized activity that produces a palpable pulse without compressions.
Not this: Starting CPR is the treatment that aims for ROSC, not ROSC itself.
Not this: ROSC does not determine neurological outcome, which depends on downtime, CPR quality and post-arrest care.
132: Not this: Placement matters because the current has to pass through the heart to defibrillate it.
Not this: Two pads stacked on the sternum send current through bone and skin, not across the heart.
Correct: Upper right chest below the clavicle and lower left side put the heart between the pads.
Not this: Two pads on the same side create a current path that largely misses the heart.
133: Not this: A tired rescuer who can still compress swaps with a partner; fatigue alone does not end CPR.
Not this: A valid DNR discovered during the call is a legitimate reason to stop resuscitation.
Not this: No fixed time such as 20 minutes ends CPR on its own; termination needs protocol criteria and medical direction.
Correct: CPR stops for ROSC, handover to equal or higher care, or a valid order such as a DNR.
134: Not this: Full recoil is done at the normal 100 to 120 rate; it does not require slowing down.
Not this: Recoil matters at every age because venous return to the heart depends on it in all patients.
Correct: Recoil lowers pressure in the chest so blood returns to the heart, giving the next compression something to pump.
Not this: Recoil is about refilling the heart, not resting the rescuer; rescuers rest by switching every 2 minutes.
135: Not this: No protocol schedules a pause every 30 seconds; pauses are kept as few and short as possible.
Not this: Pausing does not oxygenate anything; oxygen only reaches tissue when compressions move blood.
Correct: Perfusion pressure falls quickly when compressions stop and takes many compressions to rebuild.
Not this: Even brief pauses measurably lower perfusion and are linked to worse survival.
137: Not this: Diabetes is a major cardiac risk factor that speeds up atherosclerosis.
Not this: Diabetic patients are less likely, not more, to have classic crushing chest pain.
Not this: The MI does not imitate hypoglycemia; the point is that pain is blunted or absent, and glucose can be checked.
Correct: Diabetic neuropathy blunts pain signals, so MI often presents silently with weakness, nausea or shortness of breath.
138: Not this: Aspirin does not relieve the chest pain; nitroglycerin is the drug that eases ischemic pain.
Not this: Aspirin has a real and proven effect in ACS by blocking platelet clumping.
Not this: Aspirin does not lower blood pressure; nitroglycerin is the vasodilator.
Correct: Aspirin blocks platelet aggregation, limiting growth of the clot that is narrowing the coronary artery.
139: Not this: Low sugar is time sensitive and oral glucose is within EMT scope, so waiting for ALS only delays treatment.
Not this: Glucagon is for a patient who cannot swallow, and in many systems it is not an EMT drug.
Not this: Withholding sugar leaves the brain without fuel; the treatment and response are documented for the hospital instead.
Correct: An alert patient who can swallow gets oral glucose or another sugar, which raises blood sugar within minutes.
140: Correct: This is the action to avoid, because an unresponsive patient has no gag reflex and can aspirate anything placed in the mouth.
Not this: Recovery positioning is a proper step, so it is not the action to avoid; it lets fluids drain from the airway.
Not this: Watching the airway for vomiting or obstruction is appropriate care here, not something to avoid.
Not this: Calling ALS is appropriate, since IV dextrose or IM glucagon work without the patient swallowing.
141: Correct: Strokes are either ischemic from a blocked artery, which is most of them, or hemorrhagic from a ruptured vessel.
Not this: Ischemic strokes are real and are in fact the large majority of all strokes.
Not this: Stroke is a blood vessel event, not an infection, so there are no viral or bacterial categories.
Not this: Hemorrhagic strokes are real, and they are the reason aspirin is withheld in suspected stroke.
142: Not this: Aspirin is a proven field treatment for suspected cardiac chest pain; it is not a better field treatment for stroke.
Correct: The EMT cannot tell a bleeding stroke from a blocked one without CT, and aspirin could worsen a bleed.
Not this: Aspirin does act on platelets, and that antiplatelet effect is exactly why it is a risk in stroke.
Not this: Stroke and cardiac protocols differ on purpose; EMT stroke care does not include antiplatelet drugs.
143: Not this: A febrile seizure is defined by fever in a young child and is usually convulsive, not a brief stare.
Correct: A brief blank stare with lost awareness, no convulsions and a quick return to normal is an absence seizure.
Not this: Status epilepticus is prolonged or repeated seizure activity without recovery, not one momentary lapse.
Not this: A tonic clonic seizure has stiffening and rhythmic jerking, which this stem specifically says are absent.
144: Not this: A seizure years ago with nothing happening now is history, not ongoing seizure activity.
Correct: Status epilepticus is a seizure of about five minutes or more, or repeated seizures with no recovery between them.
Not this: A chronic seizure disorder is epilepsy; status epilepticus is an acute emergency happening right now.
Not this: A seizure lasting seconds with full recovery is an ordinary brief seizure, the opposite of status.
145: Not this: Opioids slow and shallow the breathing rather than making it rapid and deep.
Correct: Pinpoint pupils, slow shallow breathing and decreased consciousness form the opioid triad.
Not this: Fever with seizures suggests stimulant toxicity, withdrawal or infection, not opioids.
Not this: Dilated pupils with agitation and fast breathing describe a stimulant picture.
146: Not this: Naloxone has no effect on blood glucose, which is treated with glucose.
Not this: Naloxone does not sedate, and reversal can cause agitation from withdrawal.
Not this: Naloxone has no effect on bleeding.
Correct: Naloxone competes for opioid receptors, displacing the opioid and reversing respiratory depression.
147: Correct: Pill bottles and paraphernalia can identify the substance, amount and timing.
Not this: Bystanders help, but physical evidence often changes care and should not be ignored.
Not this: Identification matters for the record but does not decide destination or treatment.
Not this: Scene clues often change treatment, such as supporting the decision to give naloxone.
148: Not this: Heat stroke needs aggressive rapid cooling and urgent transport, so telling the two apart changes care.
Not this: This is backwards; mental status is usually preserved in heat exhaustion and altered in heat stroke.
Correct: Confusion, seizures or unresponsiveness in a hot patient signal heat stroke, while heat exhaustion patients stay alert.
Not this: A temperature alone is not enough in the field; altered mental status is the finding that marks heat stroke.
149: Not this: Exercising the limbs can trigger arrhythmia and sends cold blood back to the core, worsening afterdrop.
Correct: A very cold heart is irritable, and jostling can set off ventricular fibrillation, so movement is gentle and minimal.
Not this: Severe hypothermia carries a special cardiac risk, so ordinary handling without precautions is unsafe.
Not this: Rough handling is exactly what can trigger a fatal rhythm in a severely cold heart.
150: Not this: Injury directly under the point of impact is the coup injury, not the contrecoup injury.
Not this: Contrecoup describes blunt acceleration and deceleration trauma, not the exit path of a penetrating object.
Correct: The brain keeps moving after the blow and strikes the inside of the skull opposite the impact.
Not this: A scalp bruise is a surface injury, while contrecoup means the brain tissue itself is injured.
151: Not this: Fault is a matter for law enforcement, not patient care.
Not this: Billing codes have nothing to do with predicting injuries.
Not this: Kinematics guides the exam but never replaces hands-on assessment.
Correct: Knowing the forces involved predicts likely injuries and raises suspicion before they are visible.
152: Not this: The two differ in how injuries are found and which structures are at risk.
Correct: Penetrating trauma breaches the skin with an object; blunt trauma transfers energy and may leave skin intact.
Not this: Blunt trauma characteristically may leave the skin unbroken.
Not this: Penetrating wounds can destroy organs and vessels; severity depends on what is hit.
153: Not this: Trajectory analysis is not the EMT's job; treating bleeding and airway is.
Not this: Exit wounds are usually larger and more ragged, not smaller and neater.
Not this: Entrance and exit wounds are usually in different places, and both should be looked for.
Correct: A tumbling or fragmenting bullet often leaves a larger, more irregular exit wound.
154: Not this: A splint that is too tight cuts off circulation; it should be snug but never constricting.
Correct: Immobilizing the joint above and the joint below keeps the bone ends from moving.
Not this: Pulse, motor function and sensation are checked before and after splinting, not only afterward.
Not this: Splinting only the fracture point leaves the nearby joints free to move the bone ends.
155: Not this: Forearm fractures are splinted with rigid or soft splints; traction splints are for the femur.
Not this: An open fracture near the knee involves a joint, where traction can worsen the injury.
Not this: Traction pulls across the hip joint and can worsen a hip fracture.
Correct: A closed, isolated midshaft femur fracture is the standard indication, where traction relieves spasm and stabilizes the bone.
156: Correct: Checking before gives a baseline, and checking after shows whether the splint changed circulation or nerve function.
Not this: Waiting for the patient to report new pain can miss a lost pulse or numbness caused by the splint.
Not this: Waiting until the hospital delays finding a problem that could be fixed by loosening the splint.
Not this: These checks are a required part of every splint, not an optional step.
157: Not this: Seatbelt bruising across the abdomen suggests bowel or lumbar spine injury, not traumatic asphyxia.
Correct: Sudden chest compression forces blood backward into the head and neck, causing purple discoloration and swelling.
Not this: Traumatic asphyxia comes from blunt crushing force on the chest, not from a penetrating wound.
Not this: The hallmark is discoloration above the compression, in the face and neck, not bruising only at the impact point.
158: Not this: Broken rib ends can tear the pleura and lung, so the risk goes well beyond local pain.
Not this: Flail chest is not near certain, and needle decompression treats tension pneumothorax and is not an EMT skill.
Correct: Rib ends can cause a pneumothorax or hemothorax, and pain makes the patient breathe shallowly.
Not this: Force that breaks several ribs often injures the lung beneath, so it is more than skin bruising.
159: Not this: Fluid or blood around the heart that restricts pumping is pericardial tamponade.
Not this: Air in the pleural space collapsing the lung is a pneumothorax, not a hemothorax.
Correct: Hemo means blood, and blood in the pleural space compresses the lung and can cause shock.
Not this: A hemothorax can hide major blood loss and needs close monitoring for shock and breathing trouble.
160: Not this: Mild bruising alone neither proves nor excludes internal injury, so it is not the most alarming finding listed.
Correct: Rigidity, distention and tenderness with shock signs show blood collecting in the abdomen and ongoing volume loss.
Not this: A soft, non-tender abdomen with normal vital signs is the most reassuring picture offered.
Not this: Feeling fine with stable vitals may still be early compensated shock, but it is less alarming than rigidity with shock.
161: Not this: A tourniquet cannot be applied around the pelvis and is not a technique for genital bleeding.
Not this: Significant bleeding is controlled when it is found, not after the rapid trauma assessment.
Not this: A light dressing leaves bleeding uncontrolled, and hemorrhage control starts in the field.
Correct: Genital trauma is treated like other soft tissue injuries with direct pressure and dressings while protecting privacy.
162: Not this: Drowning is a hypoxic emergency, so ventilation is given at once, not withheld.
Not this: Routine immobilization delays airway care; spinal precautions are for diving or other trauma mechanisms.
Not this: Warming follows airway and breathing, which are what a hypoxic patient needs first.
Correct: Get the patient out, manage airway and breathing first, and apply spinal precautions only if the mechanism suggests injury.
163: Not this: Pushing the globe back can tear the optic nerve and vessels and destroy remaining vision.
Not this: Forceful irrigation is for chemical exposure and would further damage an open, displaced globe.
Correct: A moist dressing keeps the globe from drying and a rigid shield keeps all pressure off it.
Not this: Pressure on the globe can force out its contents and cause permanent blindness.
164: Not this: Rubbing with a dry cloth grinds the chemical into damaged skin.
Not this: Leaving the chemical on the skin lets it keep burning through the whole transport.
Correct: Removing contaminated clothing and flushing with large amounts of water dilutes and removes the chemical.
Not this: Neutralizing agents react and release heat, adding a thermal burn to the chemical one.
165: Correct: Current travels through deep tissue, so small skin burns can hide major internal damage.
Not this: No visible burn does not mean minor; internal and cardiac injury can still be present.
Not this: Current crossing the chest commonly disturbs heart rhythm and can cause arrest.
Not this: Skin wounds are a poor guide to the internal damage along the current's path.
166: Correct: Lightning can strike again while the storm continues, so responders protect themselves and move care to shelter.
Not this: One strike does not end the risk while the storm is still overhead.
Not this: Lightning does strike the same area repeatedly; scene safety still comes first.

233: Not this: Pelvic bleeding is internal and cannot be reached with direct pressure, so movement matters a great deal.

234: Not this: APGAR scores the newborn, not the mother. Maternal pain is assessed separately.

235: Not this: Sixty weeks is far longer than any human pregnancy.

Not this: Twenty weeks is about the halfway point of pregnancy, not full term.
236: Not this: Ambient temperature matters, but the same cold affects an infant faster because of body proportions, so size is not minor.

Not this: Infants do not make enough extra heat to offset loss through thin skin, little fat and a large head.

237: Not this: A spiral femur fracture needs a twisting force and is not an expected result of a simple toddler fall.

Not this: Confronting the caregiver can escalate the scene, endanger the child and compromise the later investigation.

238: Not this: The triangle is a validated first impression, and breathing effort and skin color can be judged reliably without touching.

239: Not this: Most vaginal deliveries finish without surgery, so a surgical complication is not an expected part of birth.

Correct: Some blood and amniotic fluid are a normal part of delivery and are not by themselves a sign of trouble.
240: Not this: Normal vital signs early in an illness do not rule out a serious problem in a patient who cannot report symptoms.

Not this: The patient cannot give a history, so waiting for one only delays assessment.

241: Not this: A gown, gloves and eye protection do not stop inhaled airborne particles.

242: Not this: The purpose is sorting patients, not making room for vehicles.

243: Not this: Refusals carry real legal and clinical weight and are never optional paperwork.

Not this: Documentation is required for every patient contact, including those not transported.
Not this: Refusal calls are among the higher-liability encounters, so they need thorough documentation.
244: Not this: Treating the first patient found meant missing a sicker one, which is the failure the scenario shows.

245: Not this: Protocols do not minimize judgment; the EMT must still recognize the condition and choose the right protocol.

246: Not this: Anaphylaxis is sudden with hives, wheezing or facial swelling, not orthopnea and ankle edema in known heart failure.

248: Not this: Beta blockers do not limit blood loss or prevent shock; they only hide the heart rate response.

249: Not this: The combination adds serious risk of profound hypotension rather than a harmless boost.

250: Not this: Waiting for full immobilization before opening the airway is a dangerous delay.

Not this: This bleeding is moderate; only catastrophic hemorrhage goes ahead of the airway.
251: Not this: Cold narrows the vessels and reduces blood flow to the area, the opposite of this option.

Not this: Cold does not sterilize anything, and a closed injury has no open wound to clean.
