252: Correct: Deceleration can tear internal organs and vessels with no external sign and normal early vitals.
Not this: Compensated shock keeps vitals normal for a while, so they do not exclude internal injury.
Not this: Triage that waits for visible injury misses internal bleeding until it is late.
Not this: A single normal set of vitals is unreliable early; mechanism stays an independent warning.
253: Not this: Feeling fine early is unreliable because adrenaline and slow bleeding hide injury.
Correct: A significant mechanism prompts closer monitoring and a fuller exam since injuries may not show symptoms yet.
Not this: Mechanism is most useful before symptoms appear, as an early warning.
Not this: Serious internal injuries often produce no symptoms at first.
254: Not this: Pregnancy can hide shock behind normal looking vital signs, so it strongly affects trauma assessment and positioning.
Not this: The uterus and fluid do not reliably protect the fetus. Blunt trauma can cause abruption and fetal injury.
Not this: Positioning is about circulation, not comfort. Supine positioning can drop blood pressure by compressing the vena cava.
Correct: Pregnancy changes blood volume and circulation, and there are two patients, so assessment, positioning and monitoring all change.
255: Not this: Tiered dispatch is widely used and accepted, not discouraged.
Not this: Structured call taking is reliable enough to match resources to likely need.
Not this: Calls differ greatly in what they need, which is why tiering has real benefit.
Correct: Matching response level to likely acuity sends scarce high level resources to the most time critical calls.
256: Correct: A field delivery involves large amounts of blood and amniotic fluid that can splash and soak clothing, so a gown is added.
Not this: Taking a blood pressure on intact skin carries almost no fluid exposure.
Not this: Helping with an inhaler does not involve splashing body fluids.
Not this: A collar on a dry patient with no bleeding needs gloves at most.
257: Not this: Incomplete or wrong dispatch information is a routine reality of EMS, not a rare event.
Not this: Dispatch information still usefully guides the response. It is a starting point, not something to ignore.
Not this: The nature of a call can change or be wrong, so crews never relax their guard based on dispatch alone.
Correct: Dispatch information can be wrong or incomplete, so stay alert on approach even when the call sounds routine.
258: Correct: In conditions like cardiac arrest minutes change outcomes, so response intervals are a useful though imperfect measure.
Not this: Response time is a system performance measure, not a billing tool.
Not this: For time critical conditions such as arrest, the link between response time and outcome is strong.
Not this: Response intervals are still actively used in system design and quality improvement.
259: Correct: A newborn below about 45 mg/dL is generally treated as hypoglycemic, and a symptomatic baby needs treatment and rapid transport.
Not this: A level of 20 mg/dL is dangerously low. Newborns do not tolerate that and can seize or suffer brain injury.
Not this: A cutoff of 80 mg/dL is above even the adult threshold and would label most healthy newborns as hypoglycemic.
Not this: Glucose can be measured in the field and is worth checking in any newborn who is lethargic or jittery.
260: Not this: Jumping to a new secondary exam skips the check on vital signs and on whether the treatment worked.
Not this: Reassessment is about changes in condition and treatment effect, not confirming the patient's identity.
Not this: Stopping monitoring after treatment starts abandons the patient just when conditions can change quickly.
Correct: Reassessment repeats the primary assessment and vital signs and checks whether the interventions given are working.
261: Not this: This reverses the terms: the patient reports symptoms, and the EMT observes or measures signs.
Correct: A sign is objective and observable, such as a rapid pulse; a symptom is what the patient reports feeling, such as nausea.
Not this: The terms are not interchangeable, since one is objective and the other subjective.
Not this: This is also backward: symptoms are reported feelings and cannot be measured, while signs are the objective findings.
262: Correct: Times matter for time sensitive conditions such as stroke and STEMI and form the legal timeline of the call.
Not this: The order and timing of events often determine treatment eligibility and are examined in legal review.
Not this: Call times serve patient care, quality review and the legal record, not payroll.
Not this: A narrative without times cannot show when findings or treatments occurred.
263: Not this: Refusing to assess delays care. A witnessed account is not required to begin.
Not this: Waiting for family delays time sensitive treatment.
Correct: With no reliable history, use scene clues such as medications, the environment and exam findings to build the picture.
Not this: Falls in older adults often have a medical cause such as syncope, stroke or low blood sugar.
264: Correct: Index of suspicion is anticipating likely injuries or conditions from the mechanism or presentation before they are confirmed.
Not this: It is the provider's clinical anticipation, not the patient's own opinion.
Not this: It is applied in the field in real time, not calculated from hospital tests.
Not this: It is a reasoning tool, not a legal document or authorization.
265: Not this: Vision loss does not affect thinking or speech, so the patient can still give their own history.
Correct: Announcing yourself, explaining each step before doing it and describing the surroundings replaces the visual cues the patient lacks.
Not this: Avoiding touch and explanation leaves the patient confused; narrating first is what prevents startling them.
Not this: The patient remains the best source of their own symptoms and should be addressed directly, not through a companion.
266: Not this: A language barrier does not remove the need for consent and a history, so some communication must be attempted.
Correct: A phone interpreter, translation app or bilingual helper bridges the gap while you still speak to the patient.
Not this: Waiting for an in-person interpreter can dangerously delay time-critical care that available tools could support.
Not this: Gestures alone lose too much detail when translation tools or bilingual helpers are available.
267: Not this: What family members report is subjective history, while vital signs and exam findings are objective.
Not this: When a note is written does not decide whether a finding is objective or subjective.
Not this: A pain rating stays subjective because it comes from the patient's own perception.
Correct: Objective findings are what the EMT can measure or observe, such as vital signs, exam findings and visible injuries.
268: Not this: Pain does not have to match appearance, and dismissing it can miss a hidden, limb-threatening problem.
Not this: A minor-looking wound does not rule out a serious process underneath, so the assessment should continue.
Correct: Pain out of proportion is a red flag for hidden problems such as compartment syndrome and deserves closer reassessment.
Not this: Assuming exaggeration without assessing further risks missing a genuine time-sensitive complication.
269: Not this: Ventilation is still required; the advanced airway only changes how breaths are timed.
Correct: With an advanced airway, compressions run without pauses and one breath is given about every 6 seconds.
Not this: Stopping compressions removes all blood flow to the heart and brain.
Not this: The 30 to 2 cycle with pauses is for CPR without an advanced airway.
270: Not this: Inhaled bronchodilators such as albuterol act within minutes and are a main treatment for acute bronchospasm.
Correct: The EMT confirms the inhaler is prescribed to this patient and that the allowed number of doses has not already been taken.
Not this: Prior doses matter; repeated dosing beyond the limit can cause marked tachycardia and tremor, so the EMT checks first.
Not this: An inhaler found on scene may be a different drug or belong to someone else; EMTs assist only with the patient's own prescription.
271: Correct: With no trauma suspected, tilting the head and lifting the chin moves the tongue off the back of the throat.
Not this: The jaw thrust is reserved for suspected spinal injury and is harder to maintain.
Not this: Cricoid pressure does not open the airway and is not a basic airway maneuver.
Not this: Any unresponsive patient can obstruct with the tongue, whatever the cause.
272: Not this: Asthma brings wheezing and usually a known history; it does not explain chest pain after prolonged sitting on a flight.
Not this: A muscle strain may hurt but does not cause sudden significant shortness of breath.
Not this: Anxiety can cause dyspnea but is a diagnosis of exclusion and ignores the clear clot risk from the long flight.
Correct: Prolonged immobility on a long flight favors a leg clot, and sudden dyspnea with chest pain fits a clot lodging in the lung.
273: Correct: Sudden sharp chest pain, dyspnea and decreased breath sounds on one side fit a spontaneous pneumothorax, which needs no trauma.
Not this: Absence of a visible injury does not rule out a serious chest problem; decreased breath sounds demand full assessment.
Not this: Anxiety does not produce decreased breath sounds on one side, so an objective finding rules out a simple panic attack.
Not this: A weak bleb on the lung surface can rupture on its own, so a lung can collapse with no blow or penetrating wound.
274: Not this: Isolated ankle swelling with no cough, fever or breathing complaint has nothing to suggest a lung infection.
Not this: Chest trauma without fever points to a mechanical injury such as rib fracture or pneumothorax, not infection.
Not this: Normal temperature, clear lungs and no cough show no sign of infection at all.
Correct: Fever, a productive cough and abnormal breath sounds in one area are the classic picture of infection in one lobe.
275: Correct: A nebulizer turns liquid medication, usually a bronchodilator, into a mist that is breathed into the airways over several minutes.
Not this: Chest compressions treat cardiac arrest and have nothing to do with a nebulizer.
Not this: The medication opens the airways but supplies no oxygen; oxygen is still given for hypoxia alongside the treatment.
Not this: A nebulizer delivers medication and measures nothing; saturation still needs a pulse oximeter.
276: Correct: A neutral to slightly extended position, often with shoulder padding, offsets the large occiput and aligns the airway.
Not this: Flexing the neck forward is what the large occiput already does, and it kinks the airway.
Not this: Turning the head to the side does not align the airway.
Not this: Sharp extension can kink a child's soft trachea, and a child's head is proportionally larger, not smaller.
277: Not this: Bright red skin is not a universal sign of good oxygenation and may reflect flushing or, rarely, carbon monoxide poisoning.
Not this: Skin color does reflect oxygenation and perfusion, which is why it is part of every primary assessment.
Not this: Cyanosis means too much hemoglobin is without oxygen, the opposite of excess oxygen.
Correct: Skin that is its normal pink for this patient's complexion shows oxygenated blood is reaching the capillaries.
278: Not this: Angina is cardiac pain from ischemia, not a skin infection.
Not this: Permanent death of heart muscle describes a myocardial infarction; angina is reversible ischemia.
Not this: Angina arises from the heart's blood supply, not from infection or inflammation of the lungs.
Correct: Angina is chest discomfort from temporarily reduced coronary blood flow, typically eased by rest or nitroglycerin.
279: Not this: A normal pressure is reassuring, but a rate of 42 still needs monitoring and evaluation, not release.
Not this: Aggressive treatment is for bradycardia causing poor perfusion; this patient is perfusing well.
Not this: The number alone is not peri-arrest; an alert patient with normal pressure is perfusing adequately.
Correct: With normal mental status and blood pressure this is asymptomatic bradycardia, so monitor and reassess for change.
280: Correct: A brief faint on standing with full, fast recovery and normal vitals is the classic syncope pattern.
Not this: Stroke deficits do not vanish completely within moments, and the trigger here was a change in posture.
Not this: A seizure usually brings convulsions and a postictal period of confusion, which this patient did not have.
Not this: Cardiac arrest means no pulse or breathing and does not resolve by itself in moments.
281: Not this: Allergic or environmental causes exist but do not explain edema in a heart failure patient.
Not this: Infection causes pneumonia; in heart failure the fluid comes from back pressure, not infection.
Not this: The direction is reversed; the failing heart drives fluid into the lungs.
Correct: The weak left ventricle lets blood back up into pulmonary vessels, forcing fluid into the lung tissue.
282: Correct: Very high pressure with headache, altered mental status or vision changes shows end organ injury, which defines the emergency.
Not this: A calm patient with mild elevation and no symptoms is the least urgent picture listed.
Not this: A reading in doubt because of technique is simply repeated; it is a measurement issue, not a clinical emergency.
Not this: A high number with no symptoms is not an emergency in itself, since emergency requires signs of organ damage.
283: Not this: Normal turgor, moist membranes and normal mental status describe a well hydrated patient.
Not this: Healthy looking skin and no complaints give no evidence of fluid or electrolyte loss.
Not this: Frequent urination alone, without signs of volume loss, does not establish significant dehydration.
Correct: Tented skin, dry membranes, dizziness and confusion together show fluid loss that is affecting brain perfusion.
284: Not this: The timing right after stopping heavy drinking makes withdrawal far more likely than an unrelated psychiatric illness.
Not this: Allergy causes hives, swelling or wheezing, not tremors and hallucinations two days after the last drink.
Correct: Tremors, agitation and hallucinations about two days after stopping heavy drinking fit alcohol withdrawal, which can become life threatening.
Not this: A hangover clears within about a day and does not cause hallucinations.
285: Not this: Cutting and suction do not remove meaningful venom and add tissue damage and infection risk.
Correct: Calm, stillness, limb position per protocol and prompt transport for antivenom are the current approach, with no suction or ice.
Not this: A tight arterial tourniquet cuts off blood to the limb and concentrates venom, worsening tissue loss.
Not this: Ice does not stop venom and adds cold injury to tissue that is already damaged.
286: Not this: Frostbite does not require hypothermia first; exposed skin can freeze while the core stays warm.
Not this: Hypothermia is by definition a core temperature problem, not an injury limited to the extremities.
Correct: Frostbite is local freezing of tissue such as fingers or ears, while hypothermia is a fall in core temperature.
Not this: They are different conditions that can occur alone or together, and they are rewarmed differently.
287: Not this: No trauma does not mean no emergency; severe flank pain can be a stone, infection or an aortic aneurysm.
Not this: A strain follows a movement or injury and does not cause sudden severe pain that comes in waves.
Correct: Sudden severe flank pain in waves is the classic kidney stone pattern, while other serious causes stay on the list.
Not this: Appendicitis pain usually starts near the navel and settles in the right lower quadrant, not the flank.
288: Not this: Bile is yellow green, not dark and granular like coffee grounds.
Correct: Stomach acid turns blood dark and grainy, so coffee ground vomit points to bleeding in the upper GI tract.
Not this: Appendicitis causes right lower quadrant pain and may cause vomiting, but not digested blood.
Not this: Viral gastroenteritis causes vomiting and diarrhea without blood altered by stomach acid.
289: Correct: A sudden worst ever headache with new neurological signs can be a brain bleed or stroke and needs urgent evaluation.
Not this: Subarachnoid hemorrhage and stroke occur in young patients too, so age never rules out a serious cause.
Not this: Most headaches are benign, but sudden onset, worst ever severity and new deficits are red flags.
Not this: Migraine aura can cause visual changes, but a sudden worst ever headache is not a routine migraine pattern.
290: Not this: An abrasion is a surface scrape and does not separate skin from the tissue beneath it.
Correct: Skin and underlying tissue torn from their attachment, as by machinery, is a degloving injury.
Not this: A closed fracture is a broken bone under intact skin, not torn away tissue.
Not this: A contusion is a bruise under unbroken skin with no tissue torn away.
291: Not this: Full thickness burns are more serious; they hurt less only because the nerve endings are destroyed.
Correct: Partial thickness burns blister and are very painful, while full thickness burns look leathery and may not hurt.
Not this: Depth strongly changes both how the burn looks and how much it hurts.
Not this: Partial thickness burns are very painful because the nerve endings are exposed and still working.
292: Not this: Surgery is for deep burns; a superficial burn heals on its own.
Not this: Doing nothing skips the cooling and comfort measures that actually ease pain and limit damage.
Not this: Fluid resuscitation is for large partial or full thickness burns, not a small superficial one.
Correct: Cooling and comfort measures are enough, because a superficial burn involves only the outer skin layer.
293: Not this: Pain that fades quickly does not fit a dislocation, which stays painful until it is reduced.
Correct: An obviously deformed joint locked in an abnormal position that resists movement is the classic picture of a dislocation.
Not this: A joint that looks nearly normal with little pain does not suggest a dislocation.
Not this: The two can be hard to tell apart at times, but a locked, deformed joint does point toward dislocation.
294: Not this: Severed vessels do not reliably seal, and a complete amputation can bleed to death without a tourniquet.
Not this: The terms mean different injuries and are managed differently.
Not this: A partial amputation is never completed in the field, because the remaining tissue may carry blood supply.
Correct: Partial means some tissue still connects the part to the body, and complete means nothing does.
295: Not this: Bleeding into the mouth and throat directly threatens breathing, so this is far more than cosmetic.
Correct: Blood, teeth and swelling can block the upper airway or be inhaled into the lungs.
Not this: Suction is an upper airway tool and is exactly what is needed for blood in the mouth.
Not this: Blood and loose teeth are a major aspiration risk, especially if the patient is supine or drowsy.
296: Not this: A neck muscle strain causes pain with movement but does not change the voice or restrict breathing.
Not this: Anxiety can speed breathing but does not explain new hoarseness right after a blow to the larynx.
Not this: A carotid injury would cause stroke signs such as one sided weakness, not hoarseness with a failing airway.
Correct: Hoarseness with worsening breathing after an anterior neck blow means the larynx is injured and swelling.
297: Not this: An object in the abdomen stays in place, because removing it risks severe internal bleeding and organ damage.
Correct: An object through the cheek can be removed when it threatens the airway, because bleeding into the mouth can obstruct it.
Not this: A threat to the airway is exactly the reason that justifies removal.
Not this: An object in the thigh stays in place because it may be plugging a large vessel.
298: Correct: Primary blast injury comes from the pressure wave; secondary comes from flying debris and fragments.
Not this: The categories exist because each mechanism causes different, sometimes hidden, injuries.
Not this: Pressure wave injuries affect air-filled organs while debris causes penetrating and blunt wounds.
Not this: Civilian explosions such as gas or industrial blasts produce the same pressure wave injuries.
299: Not this: Patients with serious internal injuries can still walk at first.
Not this: Height determines the energy at impact, so it strongly affects injury risk.
Not this: Surface matters, but a high fall onto any surface is still dangerous.
Correct: Energy rises with height and must be absorbed by the body, though cutoffs differ between protocols.
300: Correct: An untrained rescuer in the water is likely to become a second victim.
Not this: Water rescue certification is not part of standard EMT training.
Not this: Entering the water is the last resort after reach, throw and row.
Not this: The risk is high, not modest; panicking swimmers, current and cold can drown a rescuer.
301: Not this: Position matters, because a tourniquet below the wound or over a joint will not stop the bleeding.
Not this: A joint has uneven bone surfaces that do not let the band compress the vessels effectively.
Correct: The tourniquet goes above the wound, between it and the heart, and not over a joint.
Not this: A tourniquet below the wound does nothing, because the blood reaches the wound from above.
302: Not this: Transport is not held until both babies are born. Care is adapted for twins and transport proceeds when appropriate.
Correct: A second baby may follow within minutes, so a second set of newborn supplies and resuscitation readiness is needed.
Not this: Assuming only one baby will deliver on scene leaves you unprepared if the second arrives minutes later.
Not this: Twins need real extra preparation, because each newborn needs its own warming, assessment and possible resuscitation.
303: Not this: Dehydration does not explain severe headache, visual changes and swelling of the hands and face together in late pregnancy.
Correct: Severe headache, visual disturbances and hand and face swelling in the third trimester point to possible preeclampsia.
Not this: Calling it an unrelated migraine ignores the swelling and the well known link between these signs and preeclampsia.
Not this: Mild ankle swelling can be normal, but this cluster of findings is a warning sign and not a normal third trimester.
304: Correct: Sudden severe one sided pain with vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy suggests an ectopic pregnancy that may be rupturing.
Not this: Normal early pregnancy may bring mild cramping or light spotting, not sudden severe one sided pain with bleeding.
Not this: A urinary tract infection causes burning and frequency. It does not classically cause vaginal bleeding or sudden severe unilateral pain.
Not this: This combination is highly significant. A ruptured ectopic pregnancy can cause rapid, life threatening internal bleeding.
305: Not this: Ignoring the emotional side fails the patient. A pregnancy loss is a psychological event as well as a medical one.
Not this: The physical assessment cannot be cut short. Heavy bleeding, shock or infection can still be developing.
Correct: Compassionate, non-judgmental support together with a full assessment and transport addresses both the medical and emotional needs.
Not this: Treating it like any abdominal complaint misses the sensitivity a pregnancy loss calls for.
306: Not this: Waiting with no change wastes critical time. A heart rate under 60 despite good ventilation needs escalation now.
Not this: Ventilation is already adequate in this stem, so a faster rate will not help. Compressions are the next step.
Correct: A heart rate still below 60 despite effective ventilation is the trigger to add chest compressions while ventilation continues.
Not this: Compressions are uncommon in newborns, but this is exactly the situation where they are indicated.
307: Not this: Discussing possible causes on scene is speculation that can wound the family and is not EMS's role.
Correct: Resuscitate per protocol while supporting the family with compassion and leaving cause to investigators and the medical examiner.
Not this: Pointed questions about caregiver actions imply blame, and many sudden infant deaths involve no caregiver fault.
Not this: An unknown cause is not a reason to withhold resuscitation when there are no obvious signs of death.
308: Not this: No adult can hold a child against crash forces, so a child in arms is effectively unrestrained.
Not this: Adult cot straps are not sized for small children, and pediatric restraints are the expected standard in ambulances.
Not this: Crash risk exists on every trip, so a short transport time never makes restraint optional.
Correct: A properly sized and secured child restraint device gives crash protection that holding a child in arms cannot.
309: Not this: Housing status brings real medical risks, so the assessment should be thorough, not shortened.
Not this: Assuming exaggeration is bias that leads to missed emergencies.
Not this: Attributing every symptom to substance use without evaluation misses other serious causes.
Correct: Exposure, untreated chronic illness and reluctance to seek care all raise risk and should shape a thorough assessment.
310: Not this: The animal performs a trained task for the patient, so its role is part of the patient's needs.
Correct: A service animal supports the patient's function, so it stays with the patient whenever reasonably possible.
Not this: Separation removes a needed aid, and most transports can accommodate the animal.
Not this: Service animals are trained to perform disability related tasks and are not simply companions.
312: Not this: EMS is not the evidence authority, but crews can still help or harm an investigation by how they work.
Correct: Disturbing as little as patient care allows, and noting what you moved, helps a later investigation.
Not this: Formally collecting and labeling evidence is a law enforcement task outside the EMT role.
Not this: Once the scene is safe, patient care is never delayed to protect evidence.
313: Not this: Deleting the original destroys a legal record and its time stamps.
Not this: Changing the text with no trace looks like falsification of a medical record.
Not this: A known error left in place can mislead later care or legal review.
Correct: A dated, signed addendum corrects the record while keeping the original entry intact.
314: Not this: Negligence is substandard care causing harm, not an intentional act done against a clear refusal.
Not this: Abandonment is ending care improperly, while here the EMT did something the patient refused.
Not this: Treating a competent patient against a clear refusal is legally significant even when the treatment was indicated.
Correct: Touching or treating a competent adult who has clearly refused is unauthorized contact, which is battery.
315: Correct: Due regard means driving with care for the safety of others even when lights, sirens and legal exemptions are in use.
Not this: This describes the size of the exemptions, not the duty of care that due regard places on the driver.
Not this: Lights and sirens do not reduce the driver's responsibility. The driver can still be held liable.
Not this: Due regard applies most during emergency driving, when exemptions are in play.
316: Not this: Deceased patients are tagged black, not red, in standard triage systems.
Not this: Tags show priority, not whether the patient has already been treated.
Correct: Red means immediate: life threatening injuries that are survivable with prompt care and transport.
Not this: Minor injuries that can wait are tagged green.
317: Not this: A valid termination is not reversed at family request; the crew supports the family instead.
Correct: The crew documents the event fully and notifies law enforcement or the medical examiner as protocol requires.
Not this: Times, interventions and the authorization to stop all need thorough documentation.
Not this: The crew remains responsible for the scene and the body until the proper authority takes over.
318: Not this: Recertification comes from the state and certifying body, not from an individual employer's request.
Correct: Certification is kept active through continuing education and periodic recertification set by the state and certifying body.
Not this: Passing the first exam does not end the requirements; ongoing education is required.
Not this: Certification expires on a set cycle, commonly every two years, if not renewed.
319: Not this: Mutual aid is used by EMS agencies as well as fire departments.
Correct: Mutual aid lets neighboring agencies help when call volume or a large incident exceeds local resources.
Not this: Mutual aid enables help across boundaries rather than preventing it.
Not this: It supplements an agency's own coverage and is not a substitute for routine capability.
320: Correct: Pulse quality describes strength and regularity, such as strong, weak, thready, regular or irregular.
Not this: Pulse oximetry measures oxygen saturation with a sensor and says nothing about the force of the pulse.
Not this: Pulse pressure is the difference between systolic and diastolic blood pressure, not a description of the pulse itself.
Not this: A pulse deficit is a gap between the heart rate heard at the chest and the rate felt peripherally.
321: Not this: The rapid trauma assessment covers every major body region, not only neurological status or a GCS score.
Correct: It is a fast head-to-toe scan on scene to find life-threatening injuries after a significant mechanism.
Not this: The slow, detailed exam done later in transport is a different exam; this one is early and quick.
Not this: A single-region exam is the focused assessment, used when there is no significant mechanism.
322: Not this: Pulse and blood pressure alone leave out respirations and skin signs, which can show trouble first.
Not this: Respiratory rate alone tells you nothing about circulation or perfusion.
Not this: A GCS score measures level of consciousness and is not a set of vital signs.
Correct: A baseline set includes pulse, respirations, blood pressure and skin signs, with pupils and SpO2 added as able.
323: Not this: Peripheral vascular disease slows refill at baseline, so a delay may not mean an acute problem.
Not this: Cold causes vasoconstriction that slows refill even when overall perfusion is fine.
Correct: Children have healthy peripheral vessels, so capillary refill tracks their perfusion closely and can flag early shock.
Not this: Many blood pressure medications alter vascular tone and can change refill regardless of true perfusion.
324: Not this: A palpated pressure can still be obtained in a hypotensive patient and is often needed then.
Correct: Palpation finds only the pressure at which the pulse returns, which approximates systolic; it cannot detect diastolic.
Not this: Diastolic pressure is marked by sounds fading on auscultation, which touch has no way to detect.
Not this: A palpated value is not consistently higher than an auscultated one, and tends to read slightly lower.
325: Not this: The femoral pulse can be used by trained providers but is not the standard taught site for an infant.
Correct: An infant's short, chubby neck hides the carotid, so the brachial artery on the inner upper arm is the standard site.
Not this: A radial pulse is small and hard to feel in an infant, especially a sick one.
Not this: The carotid is the site for adults and children, but is hard to find in an infant's short neck.
326: Not this: Acute blood loss makes the skin pale, not yellow.
Correct: Jaundice comes from bilirubin building up when the liver or biliary system cannot clear it.
Not this: Cold exposure produces cool, pale or mottled skin and has no link to bilirubin.
Not this: Normal oxygenation and perfusion give skin its normal color, not a yellow tint.
327: Not this: A small rise is normal, but a noticeable jump with lightheadedness is beyond the normal response.
Not this: Opioid overdose causes slow breathing and often a slow pulse, not a heart rate that jumps on standing.
Correct: Symptoms and a heart rate rise on standing are positive orthostatic changes that point to low circulating volume.
Not this: A hypertensive emergency involves very high pressure, not symptoms brought on by standing up.
328: Correct: An early set gives the baseline that every later reassessment is compared against to spot a trend.
Not this: Trending is the main clinical purpose of vital signs, not a side benefit of following protocol.
Not this: The hospital will take its own vital signs; EMS takes them early for its own decisions.
Not this: Later readings are what reveal improvement or deterioration, so they add a great deal.
329: Correct: A relevant symptom that the patient denies when asked, such as shortness of breath or nausea, is a pertinent negative.
Not this: Age is a demographic fact, not a negative finding.
Not this: A blood pressure reading is a positive, measured objective finding.
Not this: Onset time is a positive piece of the history of the present illness.
330: Correct: Stable patients are generally reassessed about every 15 minutes during transport.
Not this: Every 5 minutes is the interval for unstable patients whose condition could change quickly.
Not this: Stable describes one moment in time, so the patient still needs periodic rechecks.
Not this: Checking only at the start and end can miss a problem that develops in between.
331: Not this: A field impression is a working assessment, while a diagnosis claims certainty that needs tests the EMT does not have.
Correct: EMTs form a working impression to guide care, and diagnosing a specific disease is outside their scope.
Not this: A field impression is itself clinical interpretation, and it belongs in the report.
Not this: EMTs are expected to form a field impression, so it is not reserved for paramedics.
332: Not this: Warm, dry skin with normal refill and steady breathing are normal perfusion and breathing findings.
Correct: Neck and chest wall muscles pulling with each breath show the diaphragm alone is not meeting demand.
Not this: A rate of 16 with normal depth is normal breathing.
Not this: A strong, regular radial pulse tells about circulation, not breathing effort.
333: Correct: An isolated injury with no significant mechanism and a reliable patient allows an exam focused on that injury.
Not this: A focused exam is by definition not a full-body exam, so this describes the rapid assessment instead.
Not this: An unresponsive patient cannot rule out other injuries, so a rapid full-body assessment is needed.
Not this: A significant mechanism raises concern for hidden injuries and calls for the rapid head-to-toe assessment.
334: Not this: Entering to open windows is still unprotected entry into a toxic atmosphere.
Not this: Entering for even one patient exposes you to whatever is making everyone ill.
Correct: A chemical odor with several ill people signals a hazardous atmosphere, so withdraw and enter only when hazmat says it is safe.
Not this: Several ill people is a warning to stay out, not a reason to hurry in.
335: Not this: Carbon dioxide is measured by capnography or a blood gas, not by pulse oximetry.
Not this: The volume of one breath is tidal volume.
Not this: Respiratory rate is counted by watching the chest, not read from the saturation value.
Correct: SpO2 is the percentage of hemoglobin carrying oxygen, estimated by light absorption through a fingertip.
336: Not this: Oxygen concentration of inhaled air is FiO2, a separate idea from volume.
Not this: The maximum the lungs can hold is total lung capacity.
Correct: Tidal volume is the air moved in and out in one normal breath, judged in the field by chest rise.
Not this: Breaths per minute is the respiratory rate; tidal volume is the depth of each breath.
337: Not this: Hyperventilation means too much rate or depth; shallow breaths at a normal rate move too little air, not too much.
Not this: A normal rate alone does not prove adequate breathing; shallow chest rise shows each breath is too small.
Not this: A pneumothorax is suggested by unequal breath sounds or chest rise, not by shallow breathing on both sides alone.
Correct: Minute ventilation is rate times tidal volume, so shallow chest rise means inadequate volume even when the rate is normal.
339: Correct: Suction first, or positive pressure will drive blood and secretions into the lungs.
Not this: Blow by oxygen does not clear the airway and is useless for a patient who needs ventilation.
Not this: A nonrebreather needs adequate spontaneous breathing and does nothing about the fluid.
Not this: A nasal airway does not remove blood or secretions already pooled in the airway.
340: Not this: Bagging faster against a blocked airway moves no more air and wastes time.
Not this: A good seal does not mean an open airway; no chest rise means the breaths are failing.
Correct: Resistance without chest rise despite a good seal means the airway is closed, so the head and jaw are repositioned and ventilation retried.
Not this: A cannula gives passive oxygen and cannot ventilate a patient who is not breathing.
341: Correct: The one-way valve lets the rescuer's breath in and directs the patient's exhaled air and secretions away from the rescuer.
Not this: A pocket mask has no oximeter; saturation is measured with a separate device.
Not this: There is no timer; the rescuer times the breaths.
Not this: It carries no oxygen supply, though many have an inlet for oxygen tubing.
342: Correct: An apneic patient moves no air, so oxygen held near the face cannot reach the alveoli; a BVM is required.
Not this: Apnea needs positive pressure ventilation at every age; children are not an exception.
Not this: Gastric inflation is prevented by gentle, properly timed breaths, not by giving up ventilation.
Not this: Without breathing there is no airflow, so passive oxygen cannot match ventilation with a BVM.
343: Not this: Removing the tube first may lose the only airway if the stoma has narrowed.
Not this: Covering the stoma blocks the opening the patient breathes through.
Correct: The patient breathes through the tube, so check it for plugging or displacement and suction as needed.
Not this: The mouth and nose may carry little or no airflow in a tracheostomy patient.
344: Not this: Pressure limiting is done by a pop-off valve on some bags, not by the reservoir.
Not this: The reservoir does not remove carbon dioxide; exhaled gas leaves through the exhalation valve.
Correct: The reservoir collects oxygen between squeezes so each breath can approach 100 percent oxygen.
Not this: A BVM has no way of measuring tidal volume; the rescuer watches chest rise.
345: Not this: Intubation is outside EMT scope, and the tripod position alone does not call for an advanced airway.
Not this: Patients breathing comfortably do not brace on their arms; this posture signals real distress.
Not this: The posture is a meaningful visual cue of respiratory compromise that can be seen from the doorway.
Correct: Sitting upright, leaning forward and bracing on the arms is the tripod position, which helps the accessory muscles work.
346: Not this: Routine non-rebreather oxygen for everyone is outdated because excess oxygen can itself cause harm.
Not this: A normal saturation does not rule out need, for example with carbon monoxide exposure or visible distress.
Correct: Oxygen is matched to the patient's condition and titrated to a target saturation instead of always being run at maximum.
Not this: Giving oxygen is a basic EMT skill done under standing orders without calling medical direction.
347: Not this: Smoke irritation is possible, but hoarseness with singed nasal hair points to airway burns that will swell.
Correct: Hoarseness and singed nasal hair after an enclosed fire mean the upper airway is burned and may swell shut.
Not this: Lower airway spasm causes wheezing, while hoarseness and singed nasal hair point to the upper airway.
Not this: Singed nasal hair shows heat entered the airway, so this is far more than a skin finding.
348: Not this: A dry powder drawn in by the patient's own breath describes a dry powder inhaler.
Not this: Absorption through the skin describes a transdermal patch.
Correct: Gas flowing through the chamber breaks liquid medication into a fine mist the patient breathes in over several minutes.
Not this: Injection is a different route that delivers medication into muscle or vein.
349: Not this: Unresponsiveness suggests an obstruction that has already caused severe hypoxia.
Not this: No speech, cough or air movement defines a complete obstruction.
Correct: A forceful cough with some air movement means the obstruction is partial with adequate exchange.
Not this: Cyanosis with no breathing indicates complete obstruction with hypoxia.
350: Not this: CVA means cerebrovascular accident; a central line would be written as a central venous catheter.
Not this: Leg vessel disease is peripheral vascular disease, a different abbreviation and condition.
Correct: CVA means stroke, so the old right sided weakness is baseline and only new or worse deficits suggest a new event.
Not this: A heart attack is a myocardial infarction, abbreviated MI, not CVA.
351: Not this: A strain does not remove the pulse or turn the limb cold and pale.
Not this: Dehydration causes generalized, gradual poor perfusion, not a sudden pulseless single limb.
Correct: Atrial fibrillation forms clots that can travel and block a limb artery, causing sudden pain, pallor and pulselessness.
Not this: A cold room does not cause a painful, pale limb with an absent pulse.
352: Not this: Diuretics waste potassium and magnesium, which directly affects cardiac rhythm.
Correct: Diuretics can deplete electrolytes such as potassium, producing weakness and an irregular pulse.
Not this: Long term diuretic use can easily cause dehydration and volume depletion.
Not this: Heart failure progression is possible, but weakness with an irregular pulse on a diuretic points to electrolytes.
353: Not this: Anxiety hyperventilation is fast breathing without acidosis driving it, and Kussmaul breathing signals a metabolic cause.
Not this: Opioids slow and shallow the breathing, the opposite of deep rapid Kussmaul respirations.
Not this: Kussmaul breathing is a sign of serious metabolic illness, not a normal variant.
Correct: Deep rapid breathing blows off carbon dioxide to offset metabolic acidosis, classically in DKA.
354: Not this: A TIA is a brief loss of blood flow to the brain, not abnormal electrical activity like a seizure.
Correct: A TIA causes stroke signs that clear fully, usually within minutes to an hour, and warns of a coming stroke.
Not this: Arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation can cause a TIA, but the TIA itself is a brain blood flow event.
Not this: Lasting deficits define a completed stroke; a TIA resolves without permanent damage.
355: Not this: A TIA raises the short term risk of stroke; it does not lower it.
Not this: TIA symptoms are temporary by definition, so they do not usually become permanent.
Correct: The EMT cannot tell a resolved TIA from a fluctuating stroke, and a full stroke often follows soon after.
Not this: Resolved symptoms still need urgent workup, because the highest stroke risk is in the following hours and days.
356: Not this: Sudden loss of consciousness is nonspecific and does not point to either side of the heart.
Not this: Chest pain radiating to the jaw suggests acute coronary syndrome, not a side of heart failure.
Not this: Pulmonary edema and orthopnea come from left-sided failure backing blood into the lungs.
Correct: Right-sided failure backs blood into the systemic veins, producing neck vein distension and dependent edema.
357: Not this: Hypoglycemia can cause a fast pulse, but it builds and fades gradually with other symptoms like sweating.
Not this: Sinus rhythm speeds and slows gradually; it does not switch on and off abruptly.
Correct: Abrupt onset and abrupt end of a rapid regular heartbeat is the hallmark of a paroxysmal tachyarrhythmia.
Not this: A vasovagal episode slows the heart and drops pressure, the opposite of a rapid heartbeat.
358: Not this: Oxygen is one part of care alongside aspirin, monitoring and rapid transport.
Not this: Routine oxygen is avoided when saturation is normal, but a hypoxic cardiac patient still receives it.
Not this: Oxygen does not act on heart rate; any change in rate is indirect.
Correct: With low saturation, oxygen raises blood oxygen content so more reaches the ischemic heart muscle.
359: Not this: A stomach virus explains vomiting but not deep rapid breathing or fruity breath in a Type 1 diabetic.
Not this: Anxiety hyperventilation does not cause fruity breath or vomiting.
Not this: Low sugar comes on fast with sweating and confusion, not fruity breath and Kussmaul breathing.
Correct: Vomiting, Kussmaul breathing and fruity breath in a Type 1 diabetic is the classic picture of DKA.
360: Not this: Anticoagulants impair clotting throughout the body, so all bleeding after trauma is harder to stop.
Not this: This is backwards; anticoagulants slow clotting and make bleeding worse.
Not this: Blunt head injury is the common cause of bleeding inside the skull in anticoagulated patients.
Correct: Impaired clotting lets a small bleed inside the skull expand, sometimes with deterioration hours after a minor bump.
361: Correct: Smoking, hypertension and a family history of early heart disease are established coronary risk factors.
Not this: A resting rate in the low 60s in a fit adult reflects conditioning, not risk.
Not this: Seasonal allergies and antihistamine use are not linked to coronary artery disease.
Not this: Resolved childhood asthma is a past airway condition, not a coronary risk factor.
362: Not this: Waiting for symptoms to clear wastes the treatment window while brain tissue dies.
Correct: Stroke treatment is time limited, so the patient goes promptly to a stroke capable hospital chosen per local protocol.
Not this: Transport is based on the patient's condition and consent, not on a relative asking for it.
Not this: Timing strongly affects stroke outcome, so non emergent urgency is wrong.
363: Not this: Lip and tongue swelling with wheezing already meets the criteria for epinephrine, even though the patient can still speak.
Not this: Speech shows the airway is open right now, not that the swelling has stopped progressing.
Not this: Tongue swelling and wheezing are signs of a worsening reaction, not one that is resolving.
Correct: Airway swelling and wheezing mean a serious reaction that can close the airway within minutes despite current speech.
364: Not this: Alcohol related liver disease, varices, gastritis and ulcers are common causes of upper GI bleeding.
Not this: Vomited blood in a heavy drinker may come from varices and can become massive, so it is never minor.
Not this: Starting an IV is not an EMT skill in most systems, and transport is not delayed for it.
Correct: Varices or ulcers can bleed massively and suddenly, so the EMT prepares for shock and transports rapidly.
365: Not this: Weakness and an irregular pulse after missed dialysis are directly explained by potassium buildup.
Not this: Even one missed session can let potassium and fluid rise to dangerous levels.
Correct: Without dialysis potassium accumulates, and high potassium disrupts the heart's rhythm and can cause arrest.
Not this: A patient can be fully alert right up to a fatal arrhythmia from high potassium.
366: Not this: Deep pressure on an abdomen with a possible leaking aneurysm risks worsening the leak.
Not this: Moving him to feel the mass again adds handling and pressure with no field benefit.
Correct: Once a pulsating mass is found it is not palpated again, and the patient is treated for shock and transported.
Not this: Estimating size by firm palpation adds risk and gives the hospital nothing that imaging will not.
367: Not this: Anxiety does not cause tearing interscapular pain or different pressures in each arm.
Not this: Frostbite is a local cold injury of skin and tissue, unrelated to these findings.
Correct: Sudden tearing pain between the shoulder blades with unequal arm pressures is the classic picture of aortic dissection.
Not this: A muscle strain would not produce a blood pressure difference between the arms.
368: Not this: Alcohol depresses breathing and consciousness but does not classically cause pinpoint pupils.
Not this: Hallucinogens cause altered perception with dilated pupils, not respiratory depression.
Correct: Pinpoint pupils with slow shallow breathing and reduced responsiveness is the opioid toxidrome.
Not this: Stimulants cause dilated pupils, agitation and a fast pulse.
369: Not this: The history changes monitoring and hospital treatment, so it is not just paperwork.
Correct: Mixed substances change the presentation and risks, and the hospital needs to know what was taken.
Not this: Clinical signs should drive suspicion even when the patient denies use.
Not this: Airway and breathing come first, but the substance still changes naloxone use, monitoring and hospital care.
370: Not this: Cleaning lowers infection risk but does nothing to stop active bleeding.
Not this: Cooling is not how pressure works and is not a bleeding control method.
Not this: Pressure does not numb tissue, and pain relief is not the mechanism of bleeding control.
Correct: Pressure squeezes the injured vessel, slowing flow so that a clot can form.
371: Not this: A slow heart rate would lower cardiac output further, the opposite of the compensatory response.
Not this: Blood pressure is defended by compensation and does not fall critically with the first loss.
Correct: Sympathetic stimulation raises the heart rate and constricts peripheral vessels to keep the core perfused.
Not this: Dilating skin vessels would drop pressure further, and in shock the skin vessels constrict, giving pale, cool skin.
372: Not this: Compensation can hold pressure normal through a large blood loss, so shock cannot be ruled out.
Not this: Blood pressure is a late indicator, changing after heart rate, skin signs and mental status.
Correct: A normal pressure does not exclude significant shock, particularly early, so mechanism and perfusion signs carry more weight.
Not this: A single normal reading means little, and trending repeated vital signs is how deterioration is caught.
373: Not this: A collar alone does not immobilize the spine and works only with other measures.
Not this: Extending the neck contradicts spinal precautions; the jaw thrust opens the airway.
Correct: The collar limits head and neck movement as one part of spinal motion restriction.
Not this: A collar does not control bleeding and would hide a neck wound.
374: Not this: An injury limited to muscle, fat or skin is a soft tissue injury, not a fracture.
Not this: A dislocation is a joint out of alignment, which is a different injury from a broken bone.
Correct: A closed fracture is a broken bone with the skin over it unbroken.
Not this: Bone protruding through the skin describes an open fracture.
375: Not this: One check before splinting cannot show whether the splint itself caused a problem.
Not this: Even a well applied splint can press on a vessel or nerve, especially as swelling increases.
Correct: Comparing checks from before and after shows whether splinting changed circulation or nerve function.
Not this: Arms have vessels and nerves beside the bones too, so the check applies to every limb.
376: Correct: A pelvic fracture can bleed massively inside while the groin wound bleeds outside, so both sources of blood loss threaten life.
Not this: Pelvic fractures come from high energy mechanisms that can also injure the spine.
Not this: Slowing external bleeding says nothing about ongoing hidden bleeding into the pelvis.
Not this: The pelvic fracture can be the more lethal injury, so it is never a secondary concern.
377: Not this: The pelvis is highly vascular and often bleeds more than an isolated femur fracture.
Not this: Much of the bleeding comes from torn pelvic veins and arteries, and movement makes it worse.
Correct: Moving the fragments breaks up early clots and restarts or increases internal bleeding.
Not this: The pelvis sits right beside major vessels, so movement matters for bleeding as well as for the spine.
378: Not this: Dressings have no anesthetic effect, and pain is managed by other means.
Not this: A dressing covers and protects a wound but does not clean it.
Not this: Stopping all blood flow to a limb is the job of a tourniquet, not a bulky dressing.
Correct: A bulky dressing absorbs blood and drainage, adds gentle pressure to help control bleeding and protects the wound.
379: Correct: Blood in the anterior chamber means internal eye injury, so keep all pressure off the globe and transport promptly.
Not this: Pressure on the globe raises intraocular pressure and can worsen bleeding or force out eye contents.
Not this: The blood is inside the eye, so irrigation cannot remove it and may add further trauma.
Not this: Rubbing presses on the globe and can cause rebleeding and permanent vision loss.
380: Correct: A newly dilated, sluggish pupil after head injury means rising pressure is compressing the oculomotor nerve on that side.
Not this: Baseline unequal pupils exist, but a new change after head trauma must be treated as brain injury.
Not this: A surface eye injury causes pain and tearing, not a widening sluggish pupil with suspected brain injury.
Not this: A pupil that is dilating and slowing shows pressure is rising, not falling.
381: Not this: Leaving a pulseless limb deformed lets ischemia continue, so many protocols allow one gentle realignment attempt.
Correct: Many protocols allow one gentle attempt to realign a pulseless deformed limb to restore circulation before splinting.
Not this: An absent pulse beyond a deformity threatens the limb and is never dismissed as a hard to feel pulse.
Not this: Waiting for the hospital prolongs ischemia when realignment and a splint may restore blood flow now.
382: Correct: A sign is something the EMT can see, feel or measure, which makes pale, cool, clammy skin an objective finding.
Not this: Skin signs are found by looking and touching and need no machine.
Not this: Skin signs are highly relevant and are among the earliest clues to shock.
Not this: A symptom is what the patient reports feeling, such as nausea or dizziness, not what you observe.
383: Correct: Taking a helmet off moves the head on the neck and could worsen an unstable cervical injury.
Not this: A collar cannot be properly applied or protect the spine during helmet removal.
Not this: A helmet that blocks airway management or ventilation must come off.
Not this: Routine removal adds needless spinal movement when the helmet fits well and the airway is accessible.
384: Not this: Wound size at exit or entry is variable and does not explain the hidden damage.
Correct: Current travels deep along nerves, vessels and muscle, causing damage that small skin burns do not show.
Not this: Deep muscle, nerve and vessel injury is the main danger of high-voltage current.
Not this: Small burns do not mean the current stayed at the surface.
385: Not this: Pain does limit breathing, but the question asks what the flail segment adds beyond pain.
Not this: A flail segment does not stabilize itself and often progresses to respiratory failure needing assisted ventilation.
Correct: The free segment moves opposite the chest wall, so the lung beneath cannot expand effectively.
Not this: The ribs are central to breathing mechanics, and a flail chest is a chest wall injury.
386: Not this: A dressing never replaces reassessment, because a pneumothorax can still worsen underneath it.
Not this: A chest seal cannot stop bleeding from lung or great vessels, which needs surgery.
Correct: The seal stops air being sucked through the wound into the pleural space with each breath.
Not this: No field dressing seals the chest permanently, and a total seal risks trapping air and causing tension.
387: Not this: Covering both eyes can raise anxiety, but it has a real protective purpose that outweighs this.
Correct: Both eyes track together, so covering the good eye stops the injured one from moving with it.
Not this: The purpose is mechanical protection of the injured eye, not simply calming the patient.
Not this: Covering only the injured eye lets the other eye keep tracking and drag the injured one along.
388: Not this: Life threats and limb fractures differ greatly in urgency.
Not this: A fracture is rarely the most urgent problem; airway and bleeding kill faster.
Not this: Splinting every fracture on scene delays the surgical care a critical patient needs.
Correct: Fix what kills first and move toward definitive care; lower-priority injuries are handled en route.
389: Not this: Bruises are always assessed, because they can mark serious injury underneath even without pain.
Not this: Soft tissue means skin, fat and muscle, so an injury limited to bone is not a contusion.
Correct: A contusion is damage to tissue and small vessels under skin that stays unbroken.
Not this: Broken skin with external bleeding describes an open wound, not a closed injury.
390: Not this: The due date is calculated from the last menstrual period and prenatal dating, not from a score after birth.
Not this: Birth weight and growth percentiles are measured with a scale and charts, not with APGAR.
Correct: APGAR records how well the newborn is transitioning to life outside the womb at 1 and 5 minutes.
Not this: Gestational age is estimated with other tools. APGAR looks at color, pulse, reflexes, tone and breathing.
391: Not this: Pulling on the baby can cause birth injury and skips the check for a cord around the neck.
Not this: The cord is not cut before checking the neck and delivering the baby, unless a tight nuchal cord cannot be slipped off.
Correct: Once the head is out, check for a cord around the neck so it can be slipped off before the body delivers.
Not this: The placenta delivers after the baby. Waiting for it would ignore the baby's neck, airway and the rest of the delivery.
392: Not this: A newborn who is still limp and blue after the first steps is not stable and needs help breathing.
Not this: Compressions come only after effective ventilation fails to raise a heart rate below 60, and never without assessment.
Correct: If drying, stimulation and positioning do not work, the next step is positive pressure ventilation with a newborn bag valve mask.
Not this: Withholding care lets a treatable breathing problem progress toward cardiac arrest.
393: Not this: Slower clotting is not the reason, since healthy children clot normally and the problem is their small volume.
Correct: With a small total blood volume, the same amount of blood lost is a much larger share of a child's circulation.
Not this: The risk is not comparable to adults, because children hold pressure and then decompensate suddenly on a smaller reserve.
Not this: Children compensate very well at first with tachycardia and vasoconstriction, which actually hides early shock.
394: Not this: A stethoscope is hands on equipment used later, while the triangle relies on watching and listening from a distance.
Correct: Retractions, tripod or sniffing position, nasal flaring and audible sounds are judged by observation without touching the child.
Not this: Young children cannot reliably describe their breathing, so watching their effort is more useful than asking.
Not this: Pulse oximetry needs equipment and contact, so it follows the across the room impression rather than starting it.
395: Correct: Crowning with a strong urge to push means birth is minutes away, so prepare to deliver on scene.
Not this: With crowning present there is not ample time. Transport now risks an uncontrolled delivery in a moving ambulance.
Not this: Telling her not to push does not stop an imminent delivery and is not appropriate at this stage.
Not this: Crowning together with an urge to push is the most reliable sign that birth is minutes away.
396: Not this: Cord cutting is a separate step, delayed about a minute in a vigorous baby, and has nothing to do with managing the placenta.
Not this: Transport is never held for hours. If the placenta has not delivered when mother and baby are ready, go.
Not this: Pulling on the cord, even gently, can tear it or invert the uterus and cause severe hemorrhage.
Correct: Never pull on the cord. Let the placenta deliver on its own and transport when ready, whether or not it has delivered.
397: Not this: A caregiver being present does not replace the patient's own consent unless the patient lacks capacity or has a legal guardian.
Not this: Many patients understand a great deal, and every patient is owed an explanation.
Not this: The caregiver adds history, but the patient is still the main person you speak to.
Correct: The patient is addressed directly in plain language, with a caregiver adding history, and incapacity is never assumed from a diagnosis.
398: Not this: A rate of 40 to 60 is severe bradycardia in a newborn and calls for ventilation and possibly compressions.
Not this: A rate of 60 to 80 is well below 100, so the newborn needs positive pressure ventilation.
Correct: A healthy newborn's heart rate is roughly 120 to 160 beats per minute shortly after birth.
Not this: A rate of 200 to 220 is abnormally fast even for a newborn and is not a normal range.
399: Correct: Tilting her to the left, or manually displacing the uterus left, keeps the uterus off the vena cava and protects blood pressure.
Not this: Position matters more than gestational age here. In later pregnancy, lying flat lets the uterus compress the vena cava.
Not this: Sitting fully upright is about comfort and may not suit a trauma patient. It is not the standard fix for vena cava compression.
Not this: Flat on her back allows supine hypotension. Even with spinal precautions, the board is tilted or the uterus displaced left.
400: Correct: Injuries of different ages, a story that does not fit and delayed care call for objective documentation and mandated reporting.
Not this: EMTs are mandated reporters, so noticing and reporting suspected abuse is exactly their role.
Not this: Refusing transport leaves an injured child on scene and in possible danger while nothing gets resolved.
Not this: Confrontation escalates the scene, delays care and can compromise the investigation that follows the report.
401: Not this: Vital signs remain useful in older patients when read against the patient's own baseline.
Not this: Chronic disease and medications do shift what is normal for many older patients.
Correct: Conditions such as hypertension and drugs such as beta blockers change an older patient's baseline and blunt expected responses.
Not this: Standard equipment measures vital signs in older adults accurately.
402: Not this: Keeping the animal with its handler preserves a function the patient depends on.
Correct: The service animal performs an ongoing disability related task for the patient, which is why it travels with the handler.
Not this: Service animals have legal protection and a working role that pets do not.
Not this: Leaving the animal behind is how pets are handled, not service animals.
403: Not this: Bruising in unusual places matters whether or not the child reports pain, and many toddlers cannot say.
Correct: Bruises where a child that age would not normally injure themselves should raise suspicion for non accidental injury.
Not this: Everyday bumps bruise shins and knees, so normal activity does not explain bruising in protected areas.
Not this: Waiting for a pain complaint ignores that pattern and location, not pain, make the finding significant.
404: Not this: Shoulder dystocia is not a routine pause. Each minute of delay risks cord compression and hypoxia for the baby.
Not this: The baby is at serious risk too. The cord can be compressed and the brachial plexus injured.
Not this: If positioning maneuvers do not work quickly, urgent transport is needed. The hospital has interventions EMS does not.
Correct: Difficulty delivering the shoulders after the head suggests shoulder dystocia, which endangers both the newborn and the mother.
405: Not this: The report is for preparation, not for asking permission to bring the patient.
Correct: The ETA tells the team how long it has to assemble staff, a room and equipment.
Not this: Hospitals do not bill for transport time, and the report has no billing role.
Not this: Unit availability is tracked by dispatch through status updates, not through the hospital report.
406: Not this: Encryption is about privacy, not about limiting chatter.
Not this: Repeating every transmission would add traffic rather than reduce it.
Correct: A controlled channel limits non essential traffic so critical messages get through without delay.
Not this: Radio communication continues; only unnecessary traffic is held.
407: Not this: Smoking beside oxygen is an immediate fire hazard and cannot wait until you leave.
Not this: Turning off the oxygen harms a short of breath patient when the real hazard is the cigarette.
Not this: A concentrator still enriches the air and tubing with oxygen, so the fire risk is real.
Correct: Remove the hazard first. Have the cigarette put out and kept away from the oxygen before starting care.
408: Not this: The transport officer manages destinations and ambulance flow under command.
Not this: The public information officer handles media and public messaging.
Not this: The triage officer runs patient sorting and reports up the chain.
Correct: The incident commander holds overall responsibility for strategy, resources and scene management.
409: Correct: The report records the assessment, the advice given and the refusal process for continuity and legal protection.
Not this: A verbal statement leaves no durable record if the refusal is later questioned.
Not this: Billing is a secondary use; a refusal still needs a full report.
Not this: The clinical and legal role of the report is at its greatest on a refusal, not limited.
410: Not this: Understanding cannot be assumed; the specific risks must be explained for the refusal to be informed.
Not this: A signed refusal form is standard practice and supports the documentation of the discussion.
Correct: An informed refusal requires clearly explaining the risks and documenting that you did so.
Not this: Withholding the risks makes the refusal uninformed and exposes the patient to harm.
411: Not this: An empty, buckled car seat and a diaper bag suggest a child may have been in the car and ejected.
Not this: Bystanders may not know. Counting patients is your job during size-up.
Not this: Delaying the search could leave an ejected infant undiscovered.
Correct: Ask the driver and search in and around the vehicle, because the clues suggest a possible unseen infant patient.
412: Not this: Triage is done by the triage officer and triage unit, not by transport.
Not this: The transport officer coordinates and does not provide hands on care.
Correct: The transport officer assigns patients to hospitals by acuity and capacity and tracks who went where.
Not this: Destination decisions are the core of the role, not something separate from it.
413: Not this: Waiting for a physician's call delays compressions for a patient with no valid order.
Correct: The order names someone else, so there is no valid DNR; start CPR and contact medical direction.
Not this: Family wishes alone do not replace a valid order for this patient.
Not this: Every minute without compressions lowers survival, so CPR does not wait for paperwork.
414: Not this: Many jurisdictions have validity requirements, so a DNR cannot be assumed valid forever.
Not this: Not every document labeled DNR meets legal requirements, so it must be checked before care is withheld.
Not this: Family generally cannot verbally override the patient's own valid written wishes.
Correct: An invalid, expired or inapplicable order gives no authority to withhold resuscitation that is otherwise indicated.
415: Not this: Speed alone is an arbitrary way to choose treatment and ignores which protocol fits.
Not this: Arrival order has nothing to do with which reading of the protocol is right.
Correct: Online medical direction settles a real protocol question with a documented physician order.
Not this: Seniority does not decide a clinical question about protocol criteria.
416: Correct: Accurate times guide later treatment decisions at the hospital and make the report a defensible legal record.
Not this: Treatment times matter clinically at least as much as the dispatch time.
Not this: Hospital staff cannot reconstruct a prehospital timeline they did not witness.
Not this: Performance metrics are a secondary use, not the main reason times are recorded.
417: Not this: Debriefing is not about blame, and fault finding stops people from speaking honestly.
Correct: A debriefing gives responders a structured chance to process the call and connect with support.
Not this: The PCR is still required; a debriefing never replaces documentation.
Not this: Debriefings are supportive and are not disciplinary hearings.
418: Not this: Protocols guide actual patient care and are not mainly a record-keeping tool.
Correct: Protocols give a consistent, evidence-informed framework so patients get predictable care from any crew.
Not this: Protocols apply to every certification level, including EMTs.
Not this: Judgment is still needed to recognize the condition and apply the right protocol.
419: Correct: Put on the PPE that matches the suspected transmission route before entering, because exposure starts on entry.
Not this: Exposure begins the moment you are near the patient, so putting on PPE after seeing symptoms is too late.
Not this: Waiting for the patient to volunteer symptoms defeats the purpose of precautions taken before contact.
Not this: Appropriate PPE lets a standard crew care for this patient. Handing off the call delays care.
420: Not this: Asking about the wound is history taking and gives no physical protection.
Not this: A routine laceration call has no violence threat that requires police.
Correct: Gloves and eye protection before contact are standard precautions when blood exposure is likely.
Not this: A tourniquet is a treatment used after assessment shows life threatening limb bleeding, not a precaution.
421: Correct: He felt dizzy and lowered himself with no fall or crash, so this is mainly a medical complaint with little trauma risk.
Not this: There was no fall or impact, so nothing here justifies spinal motion restriction.
Not this: The bicycle is upright and undamaged, so there was no collision.
Not this: A medical call still needs a physical exam to look for the cause.
422: Not this: Reassessment repeats the assessment after interventions to track trends.
Not this: The secondary exam is a later hands-on, head-to-toe survey.
Not this: A focused history requires questioning, and the EMT has not spoken yet.
Correct: Noting work of breathing, skin color and position at a glance before any contact is forming the general impression.
423: Not this: Pupils and glucose come later, in the secondary assessment.
Not this: Checking distal pulses in all four limbs is part of a detailed exam, not the next primary step.
Correct: After mental status the primary assessment moves to the airway, because a blocked airway kills fastest.
Not this: A full set of vital signs follows the primary assessment.
424: Not this: Unresponsive means no reaction to any stimulus, and she withdrew her arm.

Not this: Entering without identifying the hazard risks making the crew additional patients.
Not this: Vital signs come after hazards are controlled.
Not this: Many dangerous chemicals have no odor or visible vapor.
518: Not this: Severity is judged by each patient's signs, not by sharing the same environment.
Not this: This reverses the hierarchy; altered mental status is the more dangerous finding.
Correct: Confusion after heat exposure marks heat stroke, while an alert, nauseated, weak patient likely has heat exhaustion.
Not this: Confusion in a hot patient is a red flag for heat stroke and is never benign.
519: Not this: Young athletes are a known risk group, but exertional syncope is a red flag at any age.
Correct: Fainting during exertion with no warning suggests a structural or electrical heart problem that can cause sudden death.
Not this: Exercise raises heart rate and pressure, so collapsing during it is never a normal response.
Not this: Dehydration can contribute, but it cannot be assumed; a cardiac cause must be evaluated first.
520: Not this: Ice on an open wound is not a bleeding control technique and can damage tissue.
Not this: Elevation is at most an add on and does not replace pressure on the wound.
Correct: Steady bleeding from a forearm laceration is first treated with firm direct pressure on the wound.
Not this: A tourniquet is for life threatening limb bleeding or bleeding that direct pressure cannot control.
521: Correct: Hemostatic gauze is packed into severe bleeding in the groin, axilla or neck where a tourniquet cannot be applied.
Not this: A closed contusion has no open wound to pack and no external bleeding to control.
Not this: A laceration that has already clotted needs only a simple dressing.
Not this: Minor capillary oozing stops with a plain dressing and light pressure.
522: Not this: A scalp laceration is controlled with direct pressure, and a tourniquet cannot be applied to the head.
Not this: Slow oozing is not life threatening and is managed with direct pressure and a dressing.
Not this: A bruise with swelling has no external hemorrhage for a tourniquet to control.
Correct: Spurting or pulsing limb bleeding is arterial and life threatening, which is the clear indication for an immediate tourniquet.
523: Correct: Place it 2 to 3 inches above the wound, over a long bone and not a joint, and tighten until bleeding stops.
Not this: A loose tourniquet blocks venous return while arterial blood still flows in, which can increase bleeding.
Not this: It is not placed over the wound, and periodic loosening is abandoned because it allows renewed blood loss.
Not this: A tourniquet below the wound does not interrupt the arterial supply feeding the bleeding.
524: Not this: Neurogenic shock gives warm, dry skin and a slow or normal heart rate after spinal cord injury.
Correct: Anxiety, a heart rate of 110 and cool, pale skin with a normal blood pressure describe compensated shock.
Not this: Irreversible shock is the terminal stage with profound hypotension and organ failure.
Not this: Decompensated shock begins when blood pressure falls, and this patient's pressure is still normal.
525: Not this: Anxiety and restlessness are early signs seen while the body is still compensating.
Not this: A heart rate of 100 is an early compensatory response, not a sign of failure.
Correct: A systolic pressure falling below 90 shows compensation has been overwhelmed, which marks decompensated shock.
Not this: Cool, pale skin comes from early vasoconstriction during compensated shock.
526: Not this: A low-speed collision with the patient walking around is a low-energy mechanism.
Correct: High speed with intrusion into the passenger compartment transmits major force to the spine.
Not this: A same-level fall onto a hand without loss of consciousness rarely injures the spine.
Not this: An ankle sprain from a curb is a minor isolated injury.
527: Not this: New numbness and tingling is a neurologic deficit and requires restriction.
Correct: An alert, reliable patient with no spinal pain or tenderness, no deficit and no distracting injury can go without restriction.
Not this: Midline spinal tenderness is a direct indication for restriction.
Not this: Intoxication makes the exam unreliable, so restriction is applied.
528: Not this: Splinting reduces pain from movement but cannot remove all the pain.
Correct: A splint holds the injured area still, which prevents further damage to vessels, nerves and soft tissue.
Not this: A splint prevents motion; it does not restore range of motion.
Not this: EMTs do not set bones; realignment is limited to restoring a lost pulse or allowing a splint to fit.
529: Not this: Flow rate is set by the patient's needs, not by how much is left in the tank.
Correct: A D cylinder at 400 psi holds only about two minutes of high flow above the safe residual, so replace it first.
Not this: At 15 L/min it would run out within minutes on a critical call.
Not this: The first call that needs it may be the one where it runs dry.
530: Correct: Redness and pain without blisters means only the epidermis is involved, which is a superficial burn.
Not this: A full thickness burn is white, leathery or charred and often painless.
Not this: A partial thickness burn would show blisters and a moist surface.
Not this: A fourth degree burn reaches muscle or bone and looks charred.
531: Correct: White, leathery, dry and painless skin means the full skin thickness and its nerve endings are destroyed.
Not this: A superficial burn is red and painful, like a sunburn.
Not this: A blistered partial thickness burn is moist and very painful.
Not this: Even a minor partial thickness burn hurts and blisters, unlike this painless leathery wound.
533: Not this: The infant head is proportionally bigger than the adult head, not smaller.
Not this: A modified pediatric rule of nines exists and is used for infants.
Not this: Using the adult 9 percent would underestimate a head burn in an infant.
Correct: An infant's head is proportionally large, so it counts as about 18 percent compared with 9 percent in adults.
534: Not this: Scalp wounds bleed briskly because of rich blood supply, and normal alertness is reassuring.
Not this: Lightheadedness that clears in seconds with no other findings does not suggest significant brain injury.
Correct: Falling consciousness, unequal pupils and repeated vomiting together indicate rising intracranial pressure.
Not this: Minor scalp tenderness with normal mentation points to a surface injury only.
536: Not this: An uncovered sucking wound keeps drawing air into the chest and lets the lung collapse.
Not this: Sealing all four sides can trap air in the chest and turn the injury into a tension pneumothorax.
Correct: A vented seal or three sided dressing blocks air entering on inhalation and lets trapped air escape on exhalation.
Not this: Chest wounds are never packed, because gauze can enter the pleural space and does not manage the air leak.
537: Not this: A simple pneumothorax reduces breath sounds but does not build enough pressure to shift the trachea or distend neck veins.
