Not this: Tamponade causes neck vein distension with muffled heart sounds, but breath sounds stay equal and the trachea midline.
538: Not this: One simple rib fracture leaves no free segment, so the chest wall still moves normally.
Not this: An open pneumothorax is a sucking wound through the chest wall, not an unstable bony segment.
Correct: A segment moving in on inhalation and out on exhalation is the paradoxical motion of a flail chest.
Not this: A diaphragmatic hernia puts abdominal organs in the chest and does not cause paradoxical wall motion.
539: Not this: A lung contusion causes hypoxia and crackles but does not usually make one side markedly quiet.
Correct: Air leaking from an injured lung into the pleural space with intact skin gives one sided diminished breath sounds.
Not this: An open pneumothorax requires a wound through the chest wall, and this patient has none.
Not this: Traumatic asphyxia shows purple discoloration of the face and neck after crushing, not just quiet breath sounds.
541: Correct: Rigidity and distention after blunt force mean blood or bowel contents are irritating the peritoneum.
Not this: A pelvic fracture is possible, but a rigid distended abdomen means internal injury cannot be assumed absent.
Not this: A muscle strain causes local soreness but not a rigid, distended abdomen.
Not this: A surface contusion explains the bruising but not the rigidity and distention.
542: Not this: The skin wound can clot or close while a vessel or organ continues to bleed inside.
Not this: Stab wounds to the upper abdomen often injure the liver, spleen, bowel or diaphragm.
Correct: Serious organ injury and bleeding can hide behind a small wound, so treat as high risk and transport.
Not this: Probing or irrigating can dislodge clots, add contamination and deepen the injury.
543: Correct: The knife is stabilized where it is with bulky dressings, since it may be plugging a damaged vessel.
Not this: Hard to control bleeding is not an exception; pressure is applied around the object and a tourniquet is used if needed.
Not this: Removing the knife can release severe bleeding from the large thigh vessels.
Not this: Pushing the knife deeper cuts more tissue and vessels.
544: Not this: Room temperature lets the tissue keep breaking down and shortens the time available for reattachment.
Correct: Sterile gauze, a plastic bag and ice under the bag cool the part without letting it freeze or soak.
Not this: Direct contact with ice causes frostbite and destroys tissue needed for reattachment.
Not this: Ice water soaks and freezes the tissue, damaging it.
546: Not this: A standing-height fall in an otherwise uninjured adult is not a high-risk mechanism by itself.
Not this: Waiting for 50 feet would miss many serious injuries.
Correct: The 2021 field triage guideline lists falls from more than 10 feet as high risk at all ages.
Not this: Six feet is lower than the threshold the national guideline uses.
547: Not this: The platinum ten minutes refers to limiting EMS scene time for critical trauma.
Not this: Critical window is not the recognized name for this concept.
Not this: Trauma triad is not a term for this concept.
Correct: The golden hour is the idea that definitive care within about 60 minutes improves survival.
548: Not this: Waiting lets the caustic keep burning the cornea for the whole transport time.
Not this: Anesthetic eye drops are outside EMT scope and delay the flushing that stops the burn.
Not this: A dry dressing traps the chemical against the eye and removes nothing.
Correct: Immediate continuous flushing dilutes and removes the chemical, and it continues during transport.
549: Not this: Vigorous irrigation can move the glass or drive it deeper into the globe.
Not this: Impaled objects in the eye are never removed in the field, and pressure can expel eye contents.
Not this: Shielding is right, but leaving the other eye open lets both eyes move and shifts the glass.
Correct: Stabilizing the object and covering both eyes prevents movement of the injured globe.
550: Correct: Blood, swelling and loose teeth sit at the airway entrance and can block it quickly.
Not this: Severe facial trauma can kill through airway obstruction, so it is not merely painful.
Not this: Spinal precautions may be warranted, but most facial fractures do not come with cord injury.
Not this: The airway can be lost from blood and swelling alone, even without a jaw fracture.
551: Not this: A dry tooth loses its root ligament cells within minutes, ending the chance of reimplantation.
Not this: Alcohol is toxic to the root cells and kills them outright.
Correct: Milk, saline or saliva keeps the root cells alive until a dentist can reimplant the tooth.
Not this: A pocket gives no moist medium and risks losing or damaging the tooth.
552: Not this: Completing IVs and full splinting on scene delays surgical care.
Correct: Keep scene time short, treat only life threats and transport to a trauma center.
Not this: A complete secondary exam is done en route for a critical patient.
Not this: Diagnosing specific internal injuries is not possible or needed in the field.
553: Not this: Children mount a strong tachycardic response, and a fast heart rate is their main compensation.
Not this: Children are prone to hypovolemic shock in trauma because their total blood volume is small.
Not this: A small blood volume makes each loss more serious, but shock is hidden by compensation rather than appearing at once.
Correct: Strong vasoconstriction and tachycardia hold a child's blood pressure up and hide shock until late.
554: Not this: Standing on an unstable pelvis can shift the fragments and cause massive bleeding.
Correct: A pelvic binder or sheet wrap with minimal movement stabilizes the ring and limits internal bleeding.
Not this: Repeated log rolls move the fragments and break up clots.
Not this: Rocking the pelvis can dislodge clots and worsen bleeding without changing field care.
555: Not this: Patients often get sharply worse, not better, when the limb is released.
Not this: A limb that looks intact can still release a dangerous load of potassium and myoglobin.
Not this: Pressure tends to fall, not rise, as fluid shifts into the limb and toxins circulate.
Correct: Release washes potassium and toxins into the circulation, causing dysrhythmias and shock.
556: Not this: Trauma pentad is not a recognized term.
Not this: Beck's triad is the set of signs of cardiac tamponade.
Not this: Cushing's triad signals raised intracranial pressure.
Correct: Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy feed each other and are called the lethal triad.
557: Not this: Cardiogenic shock gives cool, clammy skin, often with chest injury signs and a fast or irregular pulse.
Not this: Septic shock needs an infection and time to develop, and nothing here suggests one.
Correct: Loss of sympathetic tone after cord injury dilates vessels and blocks reflex tachycardia, giving warm skin, low pressure and no fast pulse.
Not this: Hypovolemic shock gives cool, pale, clammy skin with a rising heart rate.
558: Not this: Current crossing the chest commonly causes dysrhythmias.
Correct: Heat generated along the current's deep path destroys tissue far beyond the small skin wounds.
Not this: Electrical burns are deep injuries, unlike a typical superficial thermal burn.
Not this: Entry and exit wounds are usually at different places on the body.
559: Not this: A femur fracture with an uninjured knee is suitable for a traction splint.
Not this: A strong distal pulse does not rule out traction; it is simply the baseline finding.
Correct: Traction pulls against the pelvis and across the hip, so a pelvic or hip injury is a contraindication.
Not this: An isolated closed midshaft femur fracture is the textbook indication, not a contraindication.
560: Not this: Membranes can rupture hours before birth, so clear fluid alone does not mean delivery is imminent.
Not this: Contractions 5 to 7 minutes apart suggest earlier labor, and this patient's are 2 minutes apart anyway.
Not this: Mild back discomfort is a vague early labor symptom and does not predict imminent birth.
Correct: Crowning, the head visible at the vaginal opening, is the best sign that birth will happen within minutes.
561: Not this: A cervical collar is trauma equipment carried on the ambulance. It has no role in a delivery kit.
Not this: A tourniquet is for extremity hemorrhage. Postpartum bleeding is managed with fundal massage, not a tourniquet.
Not this: An adult oral airway is general airway equipment and is not part of the OB kit.
Correct: The OB kit includes a sterile bulb syringe to clear the newborn's mouth and nose if secretions block the airway.
562: Correct: In a breech birth, let the delivery progress, support the body without pulling and protect the head, while arranging rapid transport.
Not this: Pushing the baby back in is ineffective once delivery is progressing and can injure both mother and baby.
Not this: Crossing her legs does not stop the birth and leaves the baby unsupported during an active breech delivery.
Not this: Traction on the body can cause spinal and nerve injury or trap the head. Support the baby, never pull.
563: Correct: Use gloved fingers to lift the presenting part off the cord and keep it there during rapid transport. Never push the cord back.
Not this: Cutting the cord before the baby is born removes its only oxygen supply.
Not this: Pushing the cord back in does not relieve compression and can injure the cord.
Not this: Fundal pressure drives the baby down onto the cord and worsens the compression.
564: Correct: A nuchal cord is first managed by gently slipping it over the baby's head or shoulder.
Not this: Delivery is already underway and cannot be paused. Waiting leaves the cord tight around the neck.
Not this: Pulling the head back does not loosen the cord and risks a brachial plexus or neck injury.
Not this: Clamping and cutting before the shoulders deliver is reserved for a cord too tight to slip off, not the first step.
565: Not this: Ectopic pregnancy is an early pregnancy problem and cannot explain bleeding after a term delivery.
Not this: Braxton Hicks contractions are practice contractions before labor and do not cause bleeding.
Correct: Heavy bleeding minutes after delivery is postpartum hemorrhage, most often from a uterus that is not contracting (atony).
Not this: Placenta previa causes painless bleeding before delivery, not heavy bleeding after the baby is born.
566: Not this: Back blows are for choking, not newborn care. Stimulation means gentle rubbing of the back or flicking the soles.
Not this: Drying is part of warming and stimulating, and breathing is assessed at the same time, not after a delay.
Correct: Dry, warm, position the airway and stimulate, all while assessing breathing, is the standard first sequence.
Not this: Routine suctioning and immediate cord cutting are not first steps. Drying, warming and stimulation come first.
567: Not this: Compressions are for a heart rate below 60 after 30 seconds of effective ventilation. At 80, ventilation comes first.
Not this: Stimulation has already failed. Waiting two more minutes delays the ventilation this baby needs within the first minute.
Correct: A heart rate below 100 with gasping after drying and stimulation calls for positive pressure ventilation at 30 to 60 breaths per minute.
Not this: Blow-by oxygen does not move air for a gasping baby with a heart rate of 80. Assisted ventilation is needed.
568: Not this: APGAR scores the newborn. Maternal blood loss and vital signs are assessed separately.
Correct: APGAR rates appearance, pulse, grimace, activity and respiratory effort, usually at 1 and 5 minutes after birth.
Not this: Glucose, temperature and oxygen saturation are separate measurements and are not APGAR components.
Not this: Gestational age, weight and length are growth measurements, not part of the APGAR score.
569: Not this: Circulation to skin is judged by color, mottling and cyanosis, not by tone or consolability.
Correct: Tone, interactiveness and consolability are three of the TICLS elements that make up the appearance side.
Not this: Hydration checks such as skin turgor need touch and are not one of the three sides of the triangle.
Not this: Work of breathing looks at effort, position and abnormal sounds rather than tone and interaction.
570: Correct: Small stroke and tidal volumes with a high metabolic rate make both heart rate and respiratory rate faster in infants.
Not this: An infant's heart rate is faster than an adult's, commonly well above 100 per minute, not slower.
Not this: Slow rates like an athlete's would be bradycardia and bradypnea in an infant, both ominous signs.
Not this: Infants breathe faster than adults, commonly 30 or more per minute, so a slower respiratory rate is wrong.
571: Correct: A length based tape turns the child's length into an estimated weight with color coded equipment sizes and doses.
Not this: The Glasgow Coma Scale scores neurologic status and gives no information about weight or equipment size.
Not this: Adult vital sign charts do not apply to children and say nothing about weight or sizing.
Not this: A growth percentile chart needs a known age and measurements and is not built for emergency sizing.
572: Not this: Nothing is forced into the mouth during a seizure, and this seizure has already ended anyway.
Not this: A postictal child is not yet at baseline, and a seizure with fever still needs medical evaluation.
Correct: A postictal child who is breathing adequately is placed on the side, the airway is protected and transport continues with monitoring.
Not this: Restraining limbs can injure the child and serves no purpose once the convulsion has stopped.
573: Correct: Abrupt high fever, drooling, muffled voice and tripod position without cough fit epiglottitis, while croup is gradual with a barking cough.
Not this: Bronchiolitis is a lower airway illness of infants with wheezing, and croup does not cause drooling or tripod posture.
Not this: Croup comes on gradually with a barking cough and does not cause drooling or a sudden toxic fever.
Not this: Asthma causes wheezing and increased work of breathing, not drooling, a muffled voice or sudden high fever.
575: Not this: An anxious caregiver asking for quick transport is a normal reaction to a child's emergency.
Correct: An injury that the described mechanism cannot plausibly explain is one of the most reliable red flags for abuse.
Not this: Shin and knee bruises on a walking toddler are typical accidental injuries over bony prominences.
Not this: Crying and clinging to the caregiver is normal attachment behavior in a frightened young child.
576: Not this: Confusion can limit reporting, but the recognized reason is blunted pain sensation, and confusion may itself be a symptom of the event.
Not this: Stoicism is not the physiologic reason that cardiac pain is absent.
Correct: Aging and diabetic neuropathy dull pain signals from the heart, producing silent or atypical heart attacks.
Not this: This statement compares age groups but does not explain why this patient feels no pain.
577: Not this: Many medications taken by older adults directly change heart rate, blood pressure and mental status.
Not this: No law requires older adults to carry a medication list.
Correct: Multiple medications raise the risk of interactions and can hide or imitate other conditions.
Not this: The list matters in every geriatric assessment, not only when the patient is unresponsive.
578: Not this: A medication side effect does not explain untreated ulcers, poor hygiene and weight loss together.
Not this: Pressure ulcers and marked weight loss are not normal aging.
Not this: Pressure ulcers come from prolonged unrelieved pressure and reflect the quality of care.
Correct: Untreated ulcers, poor hygiene, weight loss and a dismissive caregiver suggest neglect, which is reported per local protocol.
579: Not this: Writing is one of the most useful tools with a deaf patient who reads.
Not this: Relying only on family removes the patient's voice from their own care.
Not this: Volume does not help a patient who is deaf.
Correct: Written questions, gestures or a qualified sign language interpreter let the patient communicate directly.
580: Correct: Short, simple sentences and extra time give a patient with dementia the best chance to understand and answer.
Not this: Fast speech and jargon overwhelm a patient whose processing is slowed.
Not this: Many patients with dementia can still report pain and symptoms, so you always try.
Not this: Family adds history, but ignoring the patient loses information and dignity.
581: Not this: Lying flat can impair breathing in a bariatric patient, so position follows respiratory status.
Correct: Extra personnel and weight rated equipment are requested before the move to protect the patient and crew.
Not this: Standard equipment may fail when its weight limit is exceeded.
Not this: Moving a patient over 400 pounds alone risks dropping the patient and injuring yourself.
582: Not this: Working only in English abandons the attempt to get an accurate history.
Not this: Waiting for a relative delays assessment in a possible emergency.
Correct: A phone or video interpreter service gives accurate two way communication within minutes.
Not this: Gestures convey only basic ideas and are easily misunderstood.
583: Not this: Silencing the alarm and waiting leaves a cyanotic patient without adequate ventilation.
Not this: Replacing the circuit tubing treats the machine while the patient remains hypoxic.
Not this: Changing the oxygen setting does not help if the ventilator or airway is not delivering breaths.
Correct: Disconnecting and ventilating by bag valve device bypasses any ventilator fault and puts oxygen delivery in your hands.
584: Not this: The tube is out of position, so irrigating or reconnecting it could put fluid in the wrong place.
Not this: Reinserting the tube is outside EMT scope and can create a false tract into the abdomen.
Correct: The site is covered with a sterile dressing, and the patient is transported promptly because the stoma can close within hours.
Not this: Clamping the skin injures tissue and does not solve the problem.
585: Not this: Covering the stoma blocks the patient's airway, and some patients have no connection from the mouth to the trachea.
Not this: Removing the whole tube is a later step if suctioning fails to clear the obstruction.
Not this: An oral airway does nothing for a blockage at the tracheostomy tube.
Correct: Suctioning the tube removes the secretions that are blocking it and restores airflow.
586: Correct: Firm, direct pressure over the bleeding point controls fistula bleeding, which can be rapidly fatal.
Not this: Elevation without pressure will not stop bleeding driven by arterial pressure.
Not this: Massaging the site breaks up clot and can tear the vessel further.
Not this: A tourniquet is the backup when direct pressure fails, not the first step.
587: Not this: A valid, signed POLST is a medical order and is meant to be acted on in the field.
Not this: The form is already a signed order, so verbal physician confirmation is not needed.
Not this: Medical control does not override a valid POLST; contact is for unclear situations.
Correct: A valid POLST indicating DNR is honored, so resuscitation is withheld and local protocol is followed.
588: Not this: An advanced airway is a resuscitative measure the order declines, and the patient has not arrested.
Not this: A DNR does not mean do not treat, and comfort care is still owed.
Correct: Positioning, suction and oxygen relieve distress and are fully consistent with a DNR order.
Not this: Full resuscitation contradicts the order, and the patient still has a pulse and is breathing.
589: Not this: The time after the placenta delivers is the postpartum recovery period, which follows the third stage.
Not this: Onset of contractions until full dilation describes the first stage of labor, not the second.
Not this: Cord clamping is a procedure after birth and does not define any stage of labor.
Correct: The second stage runs from full cervical dilation until the newborn is delivered, and it includes crowning and birth.
590: Not this: Scene size-up is the broader check of safety, mechanism, patient count and resources.
Not this: Universal notification is not a recognized EMS or infection control term.
Not this: Situational awareness is ongoing attention to the environment, not the specific practice of wearing PPE.
Correct: Putting on PPE matched to the expected exposure before every patient contact is standard precautions.
591: Not this: An N95 gives no protection against chemical vapors or gases.

Not this: Downwind and downhill is where vapors and runoff travel, so that is the worst approach.
592: Not this: Arriving first or being an EMS supervisor does not give overall authority at a fire.

Not this: Rank inside one agency does not give authority over other agencies.
593: Correct: In START a patient who still does not breathe after one airway repositioning is tagged deceased, black.

Not this: Delayed patients are breathing with adequate perfusion and mental status.
Not this: Minor patients are those able to walk.
594: Not this: Standard of care is a patient care concept, not the named doctrine for emergency driving.
Not this: Reasonable force concerns restraint and self defense, not vehicle operation.
Not this: Implied consent concerns treating a patient who cannot consent.
Correct: Due regard for the safety of all others is the legal standard that still binds drivers using lights and sirens.
595: Not this: Parental consent applies to minors with a parent present, not to this adult.
Correct: An unconscious patient cannot agree, so the law presumes he would want emergency care.
Not this: Informed refusal is a competent patient declining care, the opposite of this situation.
Not this: Expressed consent needs an alert, competent patient who actively agrees.
596: Not this: The report is used on every call for handoff, quality review and billing, not only in lawsuits.
Not this: It is required documentation with clinical and legal uses well beyond billing.
Not this: It is a permanent record and can never be discarded after transfer of care.
Correct: The report is a legal document that becomes a permanent part of the patient's medical record.
597: Not this: Protection is not absolute; gross negligence or reckless conduct can still bring liability.
Not this: These laws do not create a duty to stop; bystanders may choose not to help.
Correct: They shield off-duty responders and bystanders who help in good faith from ordinary civil liability.
Not this: They give legal protection, not payment, to people who help.
598: Not this: Malice and restitution are not elements of ordinary negligence.
Correct: Negligence requires duty, breach of that duty, damages, and causation, all proven together.
Not this: Abandonment and battery are separate legal wrongs, not elements of negligence.
Not this: Consent, capacity, disclosure and voluntariness are the elements of informed consent.
599: Not this: Bending at the waist and lifting with the arms loads the spine.

Not this: Twisting under load combines compression and rotation and is a classic cause of back injury.
Not this: Lifting with the lower back concentrates force on the discs and causes injury.
600: Not this: No protocol requires lights and sirens on every transport.
Correct: A stable patient with a minor laceration gains nothing from emergency driving, which adds collision risk.
Not this: The number of patients on board does not make lights and sirens mandatory.
Not this: Saving time is not a reason when the patient's condition is not time critical.
601: Correct: Plain language is understood by every agency listening and avoids misreading during critical traffic.
Not this: Routine EMS radio traffic is not generally encrypted, and encryption is not the main communication principle.
Not this: EMS only abbreviations can be misunderstood by other listeners.
Not this: Ten codes vary between agencies, so they are not truly standardized.
602: Not this: Lights and sirens do not excuse the driver. Liability remains if driving is reckless.
Correct: Due regard means emergency privileges do not remove the duty to drive safely.
Not this: Due regard is a legal standard written into vehicle codes, and it can result in liability.
Not this: It applies whenever the vehicle is being operated, especially in motion.
603: Not this: Good Samaritan laws protect volunteers helping in good faith, not an on-duty EMT who walks away.
Correct: Leaving a patient with someone of lower training, without a proper handoff, is abandonment.
Not this: Battery is unauthorized touching or treatment, which is not described here.
Not this: Negligence is the broader category; abandonment is the precise name for improperly ending care.
604: Not this: Continuing education is training for recertification, not psychological support.
Not this: Workers' compensation handles injury claims and benefits.
Correct: Peer support, defusing and formal debriefing are the components of critical incident stress management.
Not this: A fitness for duty exam is a mandatory evaluation, while these services are voluntary support.
605: Not this: EMS has no priority to enter an unsafe scene. An injured crew helps no one.
Not this: A cautious approach still exposes the crew to an active fight.
Correct: With a fight still in progress, stage nearby out of sight until law enforcement secures the scene.
Not this: Entering alongside police before the scene is secured still puts the crew in danger.
606: Not this: Stopping an ordered infusion could seriously harm the patient.
Not this: The receiving facility is contacted and prepared before departure.
Not this: A full verbal and written report is needed, not paperwork alone.
Correct: Managing a medication drip is beyond EMT scope, so a nurse or paramedic must accompany the patient.
607: Correct: Secondary devices are sometimes placed to go off after responders gather, so stay alert and limit who enters.
Not this: Utility crews shutting off gas are routine and unrelated to secondary devices.
Not this: Unrelated alarms are not the reason responders watch for a second device.
Not this: Media arriving is not a threat and not the reason for concern.
608: Not this: A child who can walk is tagged minor, as in adult START.

Not this: Mental status by AVPU is one step in JumpSTART, not the single deciding factor.
Correct: JumpSTART uses a pediatric rate range of 15 to 45 and gives five rescue breaths to an apneic child with a pulse.

Not this: Inserting the vitals as if recorded at the time misrepresents the record and can be seen as falsification.

747: Correct: This entry records what the patient reported and what the EMT observed without judging him.
Not this: Calling the patient drug seeking is an unsupported opinion about motive.
Not this: Rude and faking are judgments about character, not clinical findings.
Not this: Frequent flyer is a biased label, and it invites the next provider to miss real illness.

Not this: A true ischemic stroke does not reverse because glucose was given, and resolved deficits still need workup.

915: Not this: A refusal driven by brain injury is not valid, and leaving would be abandonment.

Not this: Refusing all contact with police for the shift is an overreaction that harms scene cooperation.

Not this: A resting heart rate of 128 suggests the body is compensating for a problem.

Not this: Missed medications could contribute, but the fever and urine findings point to infection.

Not this: Normal lung sounds with recovery would come with relief of distress, not rising work of breathing.

933: Not this: A stroke would give facial droop, arm weakness or speech changes, not a purposeful breathing posture.
Not this: These postures make distress more visible, not less, and are signs the EMT should take seriously.

Not this: Oxygen is not universally harmful; it is essential when the patient is hypoxic.
Correct: Oxygen is given to reach or keep a normal saturation with the least device needed, which at 95 percent may be none.

Not this: Epinephrine causes tremor and a fast pulse, not stridor or hoarseness.
936: Not this: Sharp pain worse with breathing and pressing suggests a pleuritic or chest wall cause.
Correct: Crushing substernal pressure radiating to the left arm or jaw is the classic ischemic pattern.
Correct: Sweating and nausea reflect the autonomic response to cardiac ischemia.
Not this: Pain that disappears in seconds with a position change is not typical of ongoing ischemia.
Correct: Shortness of breath with chest discomfort is a common accompanying sign of ACS.
937: Not this: Dilated pupils point to stimulants or anticholinergics, the opposite of opioids.
Correct: Opioids suppress the brainstem's drive to breathe, slowing respirations severely.

Not this: Hyperthermia with agitation fits a stimulant toxidrome.
Not this: Profuse sweating and drooling suggest cholinergic poisoning such as organophosphates.
Not this: Warm, flushed, dry skin suggests an anticholinergic toxidrome.

Not this: Compartment syndrome is severe, worsening pain after injury that rest does not relieve.

Not this: Hypoglycemia means a low reading, and this glucose is 480.
Correct: High glucose, Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath and dehydration in a Type 1 diabetic is DKA.
941: Not this: Drowsiness after a witnessed seizure in a known seizure patient is postictal; stroke care fits persistent focal deficits.
Not this: A second seizure would show renewed convulsions, while this patient is slowly recovering.

Not this: Postictal confusion is a normal physiological phase and is not evidence of faking.
942: Not this: Elevation alone does not control severe bleeding and is no longer taught as a primary step.
Correct: Life threatening limb bleeding gets a tourniquet immediately rather than after a series of lesser measures.
Correct: Firm direct pressure on the wound is the foundation of external bleeding control.
Correct: Hemostatic gauze with pressure is used when direct pressure alone is not enough and a tourniquet is not indicated or available.
Not this: Waiting to see if severe bleeding slows wastes minutes in which the patient can bleed to death.
943: Not this: Equal clear breath sounds argue against a collapsed lung under tension.
Correct: Rising pressure pushes the mediastinum and trachea toward the uninjured side.
Correct: Pressure on the great veins blocks return to the heart, distending neck veins and dropping blood pressure.
Not this: A small bruise with normal vital signs is a reassuring finding.
Not this: Crackles in both bases point to fluid such as pulmonary edema, not trapped air on one side.
945: Not this: A seatbelt strain causes local soreness but not rigidity, distention and falling blood pressure.

Not this: Swallowed air may distend the stomach but does not cause rigidity, tenderness and shock.
Correct: Rigidity, distention and tenderness with a fast pulse and falling pressure mean bleeding into the abdomen.
946: Correct: Pain out of proportion, worse with passive toe stretch, and a tense calf are the classic early signs of compartment syndrome, even with pulses present.

Not this: Ordinary soreness is proportionate to the injury and does not come with a tense compartment.
Not this: An ankle sprain hurts at the ankle and would not make the calf tense or painful on toe stretch.
947: Not this: A normal pressure does not prove there has been no significant blood loss, because compensation hides it.
Not this: Decompensated shock is defined by falling blood pressure, and this patient's pressure is still normal.
Correct: A markedly fast heart rate with pressure still normal after blood loss is compensated shock.
Not this: A markedly raised heart rate after blood loss is a warning sign that needs treatment and close monitoring.
948: Not this: Pain and blistering are standard, useful field clues to how deep a burn goes.
Not this: A full thickness burn is leathery and painless, the opposite of this presentation.
Not this: A superficial burn is red and painful but does not blister.
Correct: Blisters with intense pain mean the burn reached the dermis but left the nerve endings working, which is partial thickness.
949: Not this: Normal blood pressure with no symptoms gives no reason to suspect preeclampsia.
Not this: Mild ankle swelling with normal blood pressure is common in normal late pregnancy.
Correct: Severe headache with visual disturbances is a warning sign that preeclampsia may be progressing toward seizures.
Correct: Blood pressure well above her baseline is the defining feature of preeclampsia.
Not this: Mild morning nausea is common in pregnancy and is not a warning sign of preeclampsia.
950: Correct: Limp tone and poor eye contact are abnormal appearance findings and show the brain is not being adequately oxygenated or perfused.
Correct: Pale or mottled skin is an abnormal circulation finding that reflects poor perfusion to the skin.
Not this: A playful, consolable child with good eye contact has a normal appearance, which is reassuring.
Not this: Pink skin with brisk capillary refill shows normal circulation to skin.
Correct: Retractions and nasal flaring show increased work of breathing, an abnormal finding on that side of the triangle.

Not this: Teething does not cause lethargy or a bulging fontanelle and has nothing to do with an injury history.
Not this: A bulging fontanelle with lethargy is a sign of raised intracranial pressure, never a normal variant.
953: Not this: Beta blockers slow the heart; they do not speed it up.
Correct: Beta blockers block the adrenaline driven rise in heart rate, hiding one of the early signs of shock.
Not this: Older adults develop shock readily, often with less blood loss than younger adults.
Not this: A near normal heart rate in a patient on a beta blocker does not rule out major blood loss.
954: Not this: Epiglottitis is abrupt with high fever, drooling and a toxic look, and lacks the barking cough.
Not this: A foreign body gives sudden symptoms without fever, not a two day course that worsens at night.
Not this: Pneumonia gives lower airway findings such as crackles and fast breathing rather than stridor and a barky cough.
Correct: A gradual two day onset, low grade fever, barky cough and stridor worse at night is textbook croup.
955: Not this: A change from baseline over hours is new, and dementia does not worsen that fast.
Correct: A sudden change on top of dementia suggests an acute cause such as head injury, infection or a metabolic problem.
Not this: Patients with dementia get acute illnesses and injuries like anyone else.
Not this: Family members usually know the patient's baseline best, so their report is taken seriously.
956: Not this: Rushing in on every call ignores hazards that size-up is meant to catch.
Correct: Watching from a safe distance when something looks unusual lets you spot hazards before committing.
Correct: Thinking about mechanism of injury or nature of illness before contact tells you what to expect.
Correct: Counting patients and calling for help early gets resources moving while there is still time.

958: Not this: Implied consent applies to patients who cannot express a decision, the opposite of this patient.
Not this: Res ipsa loquitur is a negligence doctrine and has nothing to do with refusals.
Not this: Good Samaritan laws address rescuer liability, not a patient's right to refuse.
Correct: Autonomy gives a competent, informed adult the right to refuse care, which is an informed refusal.
959: Not this: Minor is for patients who can walk.

Not this: Black applies only when there is no breathing after the airway is opened.

960: Not this: Walking up to the truck to read the placard puts you in the danger zone. Read it with binoculars from a distance.

Correct: Clots that form in the fibrillating atria can travel to the brain and cause ischemic stroke.

Correct: Organophosphates cause acetylcholine excess, giving SLUDGE, pinpoint pupils and muscle twitching.

Not this: Sedative hypnotics cause sleepiness and slow breathing without secretions or twitching.

Not this: Anticonvulsants reduce seizures when taken consistently; the problem here is missed doses.

Not this: Forehead swelling at the point of a blow is a local soft tissue injury.

Not this: Pinpoint reactive pupils suggest opioids or a pontine problem rather than a basilar fracture.
